The Customer Loyalty Secret? It’s Not Just About Shopping

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1852 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that imagine you’re at home one morning—settled in, slippers on, cozy.
  • Or, do you hop onto YouTube or TikTok and search for “bed-styling ideas”—slippers still on?
  • Getting people out of their slippers and into the store—again and again—is one challenge that pros like Evan Hutton, McGee & Co.’s head of retail store operations and a veteran of the industry, are taking seriously.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that imagine you’re at home one morning—settled in, slippers on, cozy. Your kids are playing in the next room. A couple of miles away, your local Pottery Barn is hosting a bed-styling workshop: You’ll learn how to layer coverlets and quilts, mix patterns, and plan for seasonality. And maybe at the end of it, you’ll get a small discount for an in-store purchase.

Do you go? Or, do you hop onto YouTube or TikTok and search for “bed-styling ideas”—slippers still on? Maybe you find what you’re looking for on Pottery Barn’s own YouTube channel. Maybe you search for some quilts like those you saw in the video, and—what’s this? A similar-looking option for less, from another brand that isn’t Pottery Barn?

Getting people out of their slippers and into the store—again and again—is one challenge that pros like Evan Hutton, McGee & Co.’s head of retail store operations and a veteran of the industry, are taking seriously. “It used to be you could just do a bed-styling class or [a class on] how to decorate a mantel, and people would come for that,” she indicates. No longer: Thanks to YouTube tutorials, the lure has to be much more compelling. The promise of social and experiential elements like gelato carts or floral-arranging workshops give customers a social and sensory reason to show up, she says. This strategy for cultivating customer loyalty is already making its way into the first McGee & Co. flagship in Salt Lake City, which opened in September.

Retails are seeing a growing interest for hands-on events, like this keychain-making activity at McGee & Co.

Shea McGee's finished keychain, complete with a monogram.

Sources indicate that “I think of in-store programming as retail theater,” says Geri Moran, vice president of marketing at ABC Carpet & Home, a longtime Upcoming York City home shopping mecca. The beauty of programming, she notes, is that it brings together “commerce, culture, and discovery.” Importantly, it doesn’t even need to produce a sale right away, either. “It can build awareness, strengthen relationships with the design community, introduce new customers to the store, and give existing customers another reason to return,” she says.

During the holiday season, ABC Carpet & Home hosts carolers at its NYC flagship as a way to “give [customers] a reason to visit, connect, and come back,” says Moran.

She points to a caroling event held at ABC during the holiday season. Those fa-la-las aren’t frivolous: They’re how ABC makes an emotional imprint on its community, even if it may have very little to do with a specific product. “The merchandise gives people a reason to shop,” she notes, “but the experience gives them a reason to visit, connect, and come back.”.

Another way to get people coming back? Introduce elements that can only be discovered in person, whether that’s through store design, specialty goods, or locally made wares. Across the industry, brands are tackling this in a few different ways. McGee & Co., for one, is planning to include regional variations on their signature design language across its outposts as they expand across the US. Syd McGee, the firm’s CEO, imagines a McGee fan encountering the store in different cities, each location informed by local culture. How does McGee do Texas versus California? There’s only one way to find out, he states.

Recent findings suggest that the business is also embracing the potential of merchandise that can only be purchased in-store. At the opening of their Salt Lake City flagship, McGee & Co. offered gardening gear, Cire Trudon candles, Match pewter, and vintage pieces only shoppable in person. Though customers may have initially come to the flagship to check out a newly introduced piece of furniture, they’ll discover that their local store can also be a resource for gifts and one-off finds from the McGee universe.

The Lawson-Fenning showroom creates a welcoming environment for clients.

Lawson-Fenning, a homeware brand that has built a reputation for California-inflected design, takes a similar approach to layering, blending their own collection with vintage they’ve found and work from makers they admire. “There’s always something they didn’t come in for,” states cofounder Grant Fenning, adding that “plenty of our longtime clients first walked in without a proposal.” While much of their consumer base encounters the brand for the first time through a designer, shoppers will often return on their own a year or two later.

According to recent reports, A retailer’s job isn’t just to showcase hero products—it’s to build a world. Which might be why Il Buco Vita, a lifestyle brand offshoot of Il Buco’s hospitality business, does around 60 percent of its business in person, despite having a website full of products. Founder Donna Lennard notes that art, antiques, and decorative pieces frequently sell more in store, while online sales skew toward more everyday kitchen and dining products. “It all comes down to keeping the discovery process interesting,” indicates Lennard. “With each person that walks through the door, there is an opportunity to introduce them to something they might not have known they were looking for,” she says.

The associates working the showroom floor help complete the picture, educating customers about the artisans, product pairings, and long-term care of pieces. But this year, Il Buco Vita is taking their world-building efforts one step further by opening a new retail flagship on Bond Street, just a few doors down from their original restaurant. This proximity, Lennard says, “creates a stronger connection between hospitality and home,” and provides a setting to present larger pieces, antiques, and collections in a more experiential atmosphere. “Customers can see how they live together and imagine them in their own homes.”.

Sources indicate that every problem, every era. Explore 100+ years of the Architectural Digest Archive, an unparalleled digital resource for research and inspiration. Start Searching.

Sources indicate that across the board, the brands interviewed for this story identified trust as the key ingredient in creating repeat customers. Cultivating it begins from the moment someone begins engaging with your team—and it doesn’t end when the credit card swipes. “The sale isn’t truly complete when the customer pays,” Moran claims. “It’s complete when the product has arrived, the customer is happy with it, and the experience makes them want to return.”.

Industry observers note that associates’ product knowledge is the first half of the equation. Customers depend on sales staff to understand not just a product, but the whole-room experience that brands can deliver. This expertise also supports conversations on pricing. In the showroom, customers can test-drive a sofa, run their fingers across different types of upholstery, and scrutinize construction alongside an associate, who can help them unpack the differences between two similar models. “The conversation then becomes less about price and more about value, craftsmanship, longevity, and whether the product is right for the customer,” says Moran. “Our team can also help identify alternatives when something isn’t the right fit for a customer’s budget.”.

According to recent reports, hutton notes that for McGee & Co., there was a deliberate decision made to refer to in-store employees as “design associates.” “When a customer comes in, we don’t want it to be, ‘Oh, let me take you over to the design concierge,’” notes Hutton. “We want all our team members to be able to start those conversations—and oftentimes finish them too.”.

Shea McGee, who briefed many of those first-time flagship associates herself, notes that education on the product forms a significant part of their training. The goal is for trainees to understand showroom furniture from the perspective of a designer, and to be able to translate that to the customer. By doing so, she says, associates will help buyers “make that connection between ‘designer led’ and our brand.”.

Studio McGee's senior-level designers host regular check-ins with McGee & Co.’s design associates to help bridge the brand's designer-led vision.

For trade-focused businesses, trust-building exists outside of a single transaction. Tyla Caccese, the founder of the 15-year-old trade-only rug organization Tailor-Made Textiles, emphasizes a practical tack. For her latest 2,000-square-foot showroom in Manhattan, “We wanted it to feel more like a workshop,” she notes. The design followed: There’s a substantial marble kitchen island where designers can spread out drawings, plug in their laptops, or work through a project over lunch.

In a recent development, this thinking was informed by her experiences in a shared space her brand occupied previously, where she noticed remote-working designers using the showroom as a kind of third place—not quite a home, not quite an office. “It’s been wonderful to see designers using the showroom almost as an extension of their own studios,” she claims. These current and prospective customers can get to know and trust the brand through proximity and natural conversation, turning to Caccese to work through ideas and feel at home, whether or not they’re there to source a rug. “I don’t want designers to feel like they need a project or a purchase order to come through the door,” she says. Showing that you can help them solve their problems is what will earn you their business. “Ultimately, what brings designers back isn’t necessarily a particular rug. It’s knowing they can walk in with an idea, a problem, or a completely unrealistic deadline and have a real conversation about how to make something work.”.

Industry observers note that once a customer makes a purchase, overcommunicate, overcommunicate, overcommunicate, says Lawson-Fenning co-founder Glenn Lawson. He says that wait times are the biggest challenge facing their business, which makes all their furniture to order. A piece can take 10 or 12 weeks to produce—and for a designer working toward an install date, that matters. “We’d rather give a realistic date and hit it than promise something faster and miss,” says Lawson. “When people know where their piece is, the wait feels shorter.” And in a pinch, those only-in-store items can help too: Never underestimate the power of a floor sample.

At the new ABC Carpet & Home store in Boca Raton, Florida, customers can explore the brand's floor coverings in a range of settings, from residential vignettes to more gallery-like arrangements.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, retailers need to recognize that in 2026 and beyond, you’re no longer just a merchant—you’re a builder of relationships. That kinship builds through events that cultivate brand affinity, solving customers’ problems together, and delivering compelling, can’t-find-it-elsewhere in-store discovery. But nurturing that connection is just as important as making it in the first place.

It has been revealed that “It’s not uncommon for our top buyers to receive a personal email from our sales team, letting them know about what we have coming up next and personally inviting them to check out latest collections,” indicates Lennard. Fenning seconds the motion: “Designers hear about new work first,” he says. “We invite them in for a new collection or a maker’s show. And when a project wraps, we want to see the photos.” The transaction might end at the register—but the relationship doesn’t have to.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Whitby Morrison bills itself as “the world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer,” supplying converted vans as ice cream trucks to drivers worldwide.
  • And now it has taken a massive step into the modern age delivering its first fully electric ice cream truck to Hocking’s dairy in North Devon, England.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The “world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer” has released its first fully electric ice cream truck, which is already in operaiton, and it notes it’s open for orders for more.

Whitby Morrison bills itself as “the world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer,” supplying converted vans as ice cream trucks to drivers worldwide.

And now it has taken a massive step into the modern age delivering its first fully electric ice cream truck to Hocking’s dairy in North Devon, England.

The truck has been operating since July, through the course of one “ice cream season.” It reportedly covered more than 100 miles a day and has done days serving up to 12 hours at a time.

It’s built on a standard Mercedes eSprinter, so it’s not retrofitted from the diesel vans that make up most of Whitby Morrison’s other offerings. The eSprinter comes in a “chassis cab” configuration which comes with just the chassis and cab, and lets upfitters build whatever they want onto the back end of the vehicle.

In this case, it also got some pretty extensive (and a little over-the-top) art all around the vehicle, highlighting the van’s electric operation.

The ice cream truck maker, Whitby Morrison, says this is the “world’s first fully certified electric ice cream truck.”.

We’re not sure what sort of international certifications are required for an ice cream truck so we’ll take their word for it, but we have seen a Rivian EDV turned into a Ben & Jerry’s ice cream truck, complete with side window, and a concept electric ice cream truck as far back as 2019. So it’s certainly not the very first time this idea has been had, at least.

And it is a good idea. As with school buses, ice cream trucks are vehicles that children are likely to congregate around. Having a stinky old truck spewing emissions just a few feet away from those kids’ lungs is the sort of thing that can expose them to a life of health problems… and we might as well not stack that on top of the sugar addiction we’re teaching them to have (hey, at least they have to get outside to chase the truck down, so they’re getting some physical activity out of it, right?).

It also opens up more possibilities for operators to serve at events where having a diesel truck running might not be reasonable, like in enclosed spaces or where quiet might be appreciated (this came up when we went to Harbinger Motors’ factory opening, where local food trucks were in attendance, inside the large factory building, and made the air quality noticeably worse).

Whitby Morrison says it’s taking orders both in the UK and overseas, with US orders just opening. To learn more, head on over to its website.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

OUR FITNESS EDITORS love to slip on cushy sneakers like the Hoka Clifton 11 for our 5Ks and hot girl walks. But on days when we're lifting heavy, doing a functional strength training workout, or have a gym sesh that switches between lifts and sprints, we turn to our favorite cross-training shoes. If you’re unfamiliar with the term, cross-training is combining different exercise modalities—like cardio, resistance training, and plyometric (rapid movements)—during a gym session. Think of these sneakers as multipurpose powerhouses. They keep your feet locked in, whether you’re deadlifting or speed walking on an under-desk treadmill.

Industry observers note that “They’re designed to handle side-to-side movement, quick pivots, and changes in direction—not just forward motion,” states Melissa Lockwood, DPM, a podiatrist at Heartland Foot and Ankle Associates in Bloomington, Illinois. “This makes them more supportive for gym workouts, classes, or sports where your foot needs stability in multiple planes, like pickleball or tennis.” On the flip side, a walking or running shoe usually only supports you in straight-line motion, Lockwood says.

In a recent development, wearing running sneakers for strength training workouts is generally a no-no (except for the caveat about the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 below). All the podiatrists I spoke with say it’s safer and beneficial to invest in cross-training shoes. That’s because they usually have flatter outsoles and thinner midsoles than running shoes to keep your feet locked in, claims Richard H. Graves, DPM, a podiatrist at Sol Foot & Ankle Centers in Long Beach, California. That way, you won’t wobble during your deadlifts and box jumps. The material of cross-training shoes is also more durable than running shoes to resist wear and tear, and has thick heel counters to help prevent ankle injuries.

Whether you're a seasoned weightlifting junkie or a runner on a mission to integrate more training modalities into your routine, read on for the best cross-training shoes you can find.

After testing dozens of cross-training shoes this past year, the latest lululemon Chargefeel 3 stands out for its impeccable support and stability during speedy, lateral movements like ice skaters, kettlebell squats, and Zumba workouts. We’ve been fans of the Chargefeel line for years, with the previous edition—the Chargefeel 2—winning the best cross-training shoe for our 2025 WH Sneaker Awards. Lululemon has since made a few tweaks that make it even better. “Despite the fact that sneaker fit and feel is extremely subjective, everyone I know who has worked out in the Chargefeel—myself included—has loved its perfect balance of stability and flexibility,” claims WH executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos, NASM-CPT.

Recent findings suggest that it’s now 8 ounces instead of 9.1 ounces, and has a lower heel-to-toe drop—6 mm compared to 9.5 mm—to help alleviate stress on the ankles and feet. WH associate style and commerce editor Shannen Zitz loves the wider build for lifting and squatting. She states her feet feel locked in and extra secure. “My feet stay securely in place thanks to a forefoot-hugging band on the inside of the shoe and a tough plastic heel counter,” says Zitz. She also notes that the springy EVA foam cushioning makes it a workhorse for walking and running.

And post-workout, it’s a great leisure kick for traveling or running errands. “I recently wore these while traveling, and they kept my feet super happy power walking through the airport and standing on long security and customs lines,” Zitz adds. Andriakos agrees, stating, “The stylish silhouette looks good outside the gym.”.

The fit is true to size, and the breathable knit upper doesn’t feel constricting when wearing thick socks (perfect for combating blisters!). Although wide size options are not available, the toes still have adequate room to spread with each step or lift. However, Zitz notes the wide outsole may feel too bulky during quick and dynamic HIIT workouts.

Read More: Every Lululemon Shoe, Ranked.

We wouldn’t recommend most running shoes for cross-training, but the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 is an exception. You can effortlessly transition from long runs to deadlifts, thanks to its balanced cushioning and moderate heel-to-toe drop.

According to recent reports, compared to the GTS 24, the latest version has slightly softer cushioning, with about 3 mm more foam in the forefoot and 1 mm in the heel, giving it a smoother, more comfortable feel underfoot. It also drops from 12 mm to 10 mm, creating a slightly more level feel. That can make it feel more stable during strength work than higher-drop running shoes.

At 9 ounces, it’s a lightweight gem, especially for those with overpronation or flat feet during agility drills. Its GuideRails technology—firm foam on both sides of the foot—keeps feet aligned during everything from Bulgarian split squats to lunges to speed walking. Plus, stiff heel padding keeps feet from sliding."These feel super comfortable and supportive for everyday life, traditional workouts, walks, easy runs—you name it," says Melissa Kendter, CPT, a functional strength coach. "I love that this shoe feels well cushioned but doesn't have a huge chunky sole, making it more appropriate for strength workouts than most running shoes.".

Because the outsole is relatively smooth (it’s built for road miles, not side-to-side gym moves), we’d stick to non-slip floors for quick lateral work. If your workouts are heavy on lifting or plyometrics, a flatter cross-trainer like the Nike Metcon 10 may feel steadier and more secure underfoot.

Read More: Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 Review.

It has been revealed that we’ve been fans of the Nano series since 2018, and every year we notice Reebok levels up its cushioning and heel stability to keep our feet locked in and comfortable during even the most intense workouts. The midsole padding is firm for balancing during heavy lifts and lateral movements, yet is still bouncy for excellent rebound during HIIT workouts and explosive jumps. The mesh material upper is also firm, keeping you steady when lifting heavy.

Recent findings suggest that MH digital designer Taryn Colbert used to prefer flat lifestyle shoes like Converse or Vans, but has since switched over to the Nano X5 for her cross-training sessions. The stiffer soles offer her better balance, while she notes that the heel counter is dense, meaning it doesn’t flex easily. However, the 7 mm heel-to-toe drop may be too steep for some weightlifters who prefer a ground-feel shoe. But it’s a pro if you like extra heel support.

The grippy outsole delivers superior traction when executing deadlifts or weighted squats, while the snug laces never budge. Colbert also notes that the breathable material helps combat sweaty feet. Just note that the fit runs tight (consider ordering at least a half-size up), and it weighs 12.1 ounces, making it one of the heaviest shoes in this guide.

Industry observers note that if your workouts focus on dynamic moves like kettlebell swings or heavy lifting, the Nobull Drive is a gem. It’s crafted with a breathable mesh knit upper that feels sock-like and keeps feet cool during grueling reps.

The balance of flexibility and firmness makes it simple to transition from the squat rack to the HIIT studio. WH associate editor Olivia Luppino wears them during physical therapy to help maintain balance when doing Bosu ball squats, and then hits the gym to do deadlifts. She also notes the mesh isn’t scratchy—an issue she has had when wearing this material.

The subtle foam feels similar to a minimally-cushioned running shoe, while the low 4 mm drop keeps Luppino grounded when deadlifting. She also notes that a firm heel counter makes her feet feel secure without too much stiffness. And at 8.3 ounces, it’s the lightest shoe in this guide, which makes it an optimal choice for sprints and mixed-modality workouts.

It has been revealed that nike’s latest Metcon 10 is a top pick among our editors when it comes to pumping iron. Its main update compared to the last iteration is a smaller, stiffer plate strategically placed under the heel to help stabilize the feet when squatting heavy reps or doing deadlifts. Heel-to-toe drop refers to the height difference between the heel and the forefoot of the shoe.

It has been revealed that DWF Labs reported on Nov. 19 that Bitcoin fell on 77% of US trading days when QQQ, an ETF that tracks the Nasdaq-100, lost at least 1%.

The analysis covers the period from the start of US spot Bitcoin ETF trading on Jan. 11, 2024, through Nov. 13, 2026. DWF put Bitcoin’s average decline on large Nasdaq down days at about 2%.

According to recent reports, in the Federal Reserve’s October meeting minutes, released Nov. 18, almost all participants discussed what could happen if returns on artificial intelligence investments disappointed. Most pointed to rapid growth in AI-related debt and the complex, opaque structures used to finance much of it.

Sources indicate that from September 2025 through the end of the study’s data on Nov. 13, the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) gained 85% while Bitcoin fell 39%, according to DWF Labs.

If an AI selloff spreads from chip stocks to the wider Nasdaq-100, Bitcoin’s record on those down days becomes more relevant than its trading during the chip rally.

Industry observers note that at the Oct. 27-28 meeting, many participants discussed the potential consequences of AI-related assets losing value if investors became less confident about the returns.

A few noted that exposure was becoming concentrated among a small number of firms, raising questions about how the buildout was financed and what the projects themselves might earn.

Fed staff flagged two structures that could amplify losses if returns disappointed.

One was off-balance-sheet leases, which can leave firms committed to future payments that do not appear on their balance sheets. The other was circular financing among AI-related firms, which ties their funding to one another.

It has been revealed that investors who borrowed to buy assets might have to sell holdings to reduce their debt, while fund managers might also need to sell to meet withdrawals. In the most severe scenarios, sales by vehicles such as hedge funds, bond mutual funds and target-date funds could make it harder for markets to absorb trades.

Elevated asset valuations and hedge fund leverage were the biggest vulnerabilities in the staff assessment. Strong bank and household balance sheets offered a buffer against more severe outcomes, and several participants noted the staff’s finding that banks were well capitalized.

Some participants saw gaps in the picture, and several questioned whether supervisors had enough data on banks’ indirect exposure through nonbank institutions, such as credit lines to private credit funds.

The minutes describe a stress scenario in which an asset-price decline compounds through financing commitments, leverage and the need to raise cash.

The connection for Bitcoin investors would depend on whether those pressures move beyond AI-related firms and pull down the wider market.

DWF Labs measured Bitcoin’s performance on days when a fund tracking the Nasdaq-100 dropped at least 1%.

The report found a similar pattern before US spot Bitcoin ETFs began trading. From 2020 until the January 2024 launch, Bitcoin fell on 74% of the Nasdaq-100 proxy’s large down days, and it fell on 77% from the launch through Nov. 13, 2026.

Yahoo Finance’s adjusted closes show 91 Bitcoin declines across 118 days when QQQ fell at least 1% in the latter period. Bitcoin’s average log return across all 118 days was -1.93%, including days when Bitcoin rose or held steady as well as days when it fell.

QQQ’s return runs from the prior US trading session’s close. Bitcoin’s return runs across consecutive calendar-day closes, with its daily candle ending at midnight UTC, three to four hours after the US stock market closes.

Closing prices alone don't capture the order of moves, and Bitcoin can keep moving for several hours after the US trading session ends, so the comparison includes part of that post-close window.

CryptoSlate compared QQQ and Bitcoin adjusted closes on the same dates using Yahoo Finance data.

Bitcoin closed lower on more than three quarters of the qualifying sessions.

In a recent development, sessions qualified when QQQ’s daily log return was −1% or lower, regardless of cause. Bitcoin closes at midnight UTC, several hours after U.S. equities.

Divide 91 Bitcoin declines by 118, rounded to 77.1%. The remaining 27 sessions equal 118 minus 91. Bar widths are proportional.

Sessions qualified when QQQ’s daily log return was −1% or lower, regardless of cause. Bitcoin closes at midnight UTC, several hours after U.S. equities.

In a recent development, DWF’s results subtracted QQQ’s daily return from Bitcoin’s and SOXX’s returns. On that measure, the two had a correlation of negative 0.30 from March 2026 through the end of the sample. When chip stocks beat the Nasdaq-100 proxy, Bitcoin tended to lag it.

From September 2025 through Nov. 13, the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) gained 85% and Bitcoin fell 39%.

A separate analysis by Block Scholes researcher Thahbib Rahman found that broader market moves explained part of a recent Bitcoin decline. His firm found little evidence that investors sold Bitcoin specifically to buy AI assets.

The Fed held rates in October, and almost all participants judged further increases likely under their baseline outlooks.

US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October from September, and the advance estimate demonstrated nominal retail and food services sales up 0.2%, within its margin of error, while industrial production fell 0.4%.

In the Philadelphia Fed’s November manufacturing survey, regional activity fell to 6.3 from 20.9 as the prices-received index rose to 47.0, the highest since June 2022.

Investors should watch whether declines spread across the Nasdaq-100 and how Treasury yields and the Fed rate outlook respond.

After Launching McGee & Co., Shea McGee Shares 8 Lessons for Opening a Store

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1294 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, speaking to you now, on the other side of its debut, there are some things we only learned through actually doing.
  • Industry observers note that it was important to us that the shop feel like the homes we create for our clients—layered and collected, with a variety of patterns and objects for your eye to explore.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that my husband Syd and I are both lovers of retail, and have always known one day we’d have a McGee & Co. shop of our own. Over the years, we’ve spent a lot of time jotting down ideas for our own store. Our fresh flagship is a repository for all that knowledge that we’ve been squirreling away—but it also taught us a few lessons of its own.

According to recent reports, speaking to you now, on the other side of its debut, there are some things we only learned through actually doing. From the importance of developing a training manual to the do-or-die value of a soft launch, here are eight hard-won learnings from our McGee & Co. store launch.

Industry observers note that it was important to us that the shop feel like the homes we create for our clients—layered and collected, with a variety of patterns and objects for your eye to explore. Despite the fact that the dollars-per-square-foot model is the traditional method of conceiving an in-store assortment, it was more important for us to remain true to ourselves with this first location: we’re a designer-led brand, not a merchant-led one.

Industry observers note that “I’m getting to see our products through latest eyes—and I was the one that concepted them!” states Shea. “When you see them in a store setting, pieces can have a lot more detail than you can see online.”.

It has been revealed that we started by coming up with the sections we envisioned, like a kids’ area, a kitchen zone, and so on. Then we created planograms to see how much we could actually fit, and reconciled with our merchandising team to see what made business sense. Sometimes, that meant pivoting from the early vision. A lighting gallery we had planned, for instance, ended up shifting: We loved the idea, but when we looked at the percentage of lighting to the rest of our sales, we could see clearly that it was a smarter business decision to use this space to showcase more furniture. Instead of the sprawling lighting gallery we had imagined, we created a moody lounge area that can flex to showcase different pieces.

According to recent reports, we don’t think small: Our aspirations are to grow nationwide. But however much we scale, it’s critical that we not lose the warm, personal feeling that comes from a standalone store. As McGee & Co. grows its brick-and-mortar operation, that’s one of my biggest goals. And there’s another layer here, too: Being a personality-led business, the team members in our store aren’t just representing our brand—they’re representing me, for better or worse. The design world can sometimes feel closed-off and unapproachable, and it’s always been the McGee mantra—in our content, in our personality on social media, in how we work with clients—to be warm and accessible. Now that attitude needs to trickle down to our store associates, too.

Syd and Shea McGee in their office.

It has been revealed that before we opened, I spent months developing a comprehensive training guide for our associates. It’s essentially Design 101, McGee-style, covering everything from how many inches I place a rug away from a wall, to how to pair and arrange accent tables, to how to layer bedding. We cover every level of the decorating process. Thank goodness for AI—it’s been a lifesaver: I’ll narrate as we go on our walk-throughs, and use those notes as the basis for the training manual. And it’s not a one-and-done deal. We’ll continue to add to this document as we evolve and grow.

Every concern, every era. Explore 100+ years of the Architectural Digest Archive, an unparalleled digital resource for research and inspiration. Start Searching.

Having that Design 101 established is a first step, but how do you ensure that the team is really internalizing the lessons? For us, the answer was checkpoints. As our design associates go through training and familiarize themselves with our ways of doing things, we hold check-ins with them to make sure that they’re absorbing our ways of operating. It’s the exact same as we do for the junior interior designers at Studio McGee: The checkpoints allow us to build up mutual confidence, with the aim for them to eventually fly on their own.

Shea plans to have the studio’s senior-level designers hosting regular check-ins with the shop’s design associates.

Personally dropping in myself can serve as another kind of checkpoint, too. With the flagship local, I’m able to stop by regularly in these early days to make sure that our standards are upheld, that our visuals are tight, and the operation is humming. That won’t work for us in every location, but it’s certainly a perk of opening up in our own hometown.

As much as I love a good blueprint, there’s nothing like real-time feedback to show you what’s working and what’s not. Which is why we kicked off our flagship back in September with a whisper and not a bang. We did a very soft launch with no announcement, no social post. We just opened the doors. As folks wandered in, we learned, and we tweaked. And two weeks later, we opened officially. That soft-launch period was vital for us in getting the kinks out.

One benefit of having had an ecommerce business for so long is that we have rich data on exactly where our customers are. That means that from day one, we already know where we need to open next. While launching in Salt Lake City was a logical place for our flagship, we’re already thinking ahead to how we’ll expand to some of our other biggest markets, like Texas and California.

Located in Salt Lake City’s Trolley Square, the “shop,” as Shea calls it, is 7,500 square feet.

Sources indicate that we want to capitalize on the fact that the retail-ecommerce loop is an advantageous cycle: Where you have a retail store, your ecommerce sales lift. People who are aware of your product can go see it in person, give it a sit test, think about it, and then finish the sale online. In store, we can educate them, give them styling suggestions, and show off the quality of the product in ways we can’t online. Even for us, we’re discovering new things about our assortment by merchandising it in the store—we’re seeing it with fresh eyes, and we know our customers will too.

Aside from the obvious metric of profitability, to me, success in these early days means nailing down our systems and processes. It’s not the most glamorous side of this business, but it’s a must. I want to be able to say that we know what it takes to run a store and to make the shopper experience in it as smooth as possible. For instance, I want customers to know how to get to our free design services, and to have a great experience using them. If we can do that, we know we’re on our way to some of our loftier goals, too.

I’m not under any illusions here: This first store is a baptism by fire. Not only are we opening a flagship and planting seeds for our future locations—we’re also doing it in Q4, right before the holidays. But my hope is that at the end of it, we can catch our breath and take a moment to reflect on what worked, what didn’t, and then get to work fixing it. In this business, honesty with yourself is the only way up.

“The kitchen is a working kitchen,” says Shea, who envisions cooking demos and community events enlivening the space.

Greg Guttas, head of over-the-counter trading at Flowdesk, told CryptoSlate that the desk could pay with its own stablecoins and settle with the client later against the fund holding.

Securitize and Ethena opened a new route for fund holders on Nov. 12 with a facility for BlackRock’s USD Institutional Digital Liquidity Fund (BUIDL) that exchanges fund shares for stablecoins outside banking hours. That gives eligible investors a way to raise trading cash themselves.

In Guttas’s example, a dealer would supply the cash for the Bitcoin purchase upfront.

Sources indicate that the question of what dealers can spend is sharper after a drop in stablecoin supply. Glassnode reported that aggregate stablecoin supply fell $14.2 billion in the 30 days through Nov. 9, the fastest contraction since June 2022.

The marketwide total leaves open how much an individual desk has on hand and what it would commit to a client’s trade.

Guttas described how an over-the-counter desk could handle a purchase for a client holding tokenized money-market fund shares:.

“The market maker in that scenario could use their own stablecoin balances to buy the BTC immediately and then redeem the tokenized MM funds after the fact.”.

That sequence would give the client time to settle using the fund position, while the dealer would spend the stablecoins first and wait for settlement to recover them. Until then, those funds would be unavailable for another purchase.

Sources indicate that the longer it takes to turn fund shares into settlement cash, the longer the desk has to carry the exposure. Guttas remarked larger conversions can hit size limits, and weekends can complicate access.

In January 2025, QCP disclosed that it facilitated a six-month Bitcoin basis trade for Securitize Credit using BUIDL as collateral.

A basis trade aims to capture the difference between spot and futures prices, but QCP’s account leaves the funding currency for the Bitcoin leg and the settlement timing undisclosed.

The Securitize and Ethena facility works in both directions for BUIDL. Eligible investors can exchange their fund shares for supported stablecoins, including USDC, or use those stablecoins to acquire BUIDL.

That route can give a fund holder cash to trade on a weekend.

Recent findings suggest that the facility opened with $50 million of inventory, split between $25 million in USDC and $25 million in BUIDL. Securitize stated up to another $50 million may become available within about an hour as liquidity is used, subject to terms and availability, bringing the maximum facility capacity to $100 million.

The relevant starting figure for a holder seeking stablecoins at launch was the $25 million in USDC, while the BUIDL side of the inventory serves investors converting stablecoins into fund shares.

The quoted size depends on the liquidity approved counterparties offer when an investor asks. Once a quoted swap executes, both sides settle together on-chain.

Katana CEO Matthew Fisher told CryptoSlate he looks at exchange balances, stablecoins posted as collateral in lending and perpetual futures markets, and how much traders borrow against them.

Juiced unveils another lower-cost moto-styled electric bike: Scrambler Core

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1004 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that juiced Bikes is expanding its recently relaunched Scrambler lineup with a new, more affordable model known as the Juiced Scrambler Core.
  • The new Scrambler Core starts at $1,399, compared to $1,699 for the existing Scrambler Hardtail.
  • Juiced is also offering a $1,599 long-range version of the Core, as well as a smaller “Midsize” frame that should make the bike much more accessible to shorter riders – and, perhaps more importantly, teenagers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that juiced Bikes is expanding its recently relaunched Scrambler lineup with a new, more affordable model known as the Juiced Scrambler Core. The new bike keeps much of the moto-inspired styling and performance of the existing Scrambler Hardtail, but trims back several components to knock several hundred dollars off the price.

The new Scrambler Core starts at $1,399, compared to $1,699 for the existing Scrambler Hardtail.

Juiced is also offering a $1,599 long-range version of the Core, as well as a smaller “Midsize” frame that should make the bike much more accessible to shorter riders – and, perhaps more importantly, teenagers.

In a recent development, teens are a major part of the moto-style e-bike market, and Juiced has designed its Scrambler e-bikes as a safer option for those younger riders. In addition to ensuring street-legal performance for most major markets, Juiced rolled out a feature known as Speed Lock, which is essentially a parental control option that lets a parent or guardian set a lower speed limit using a PIN code that prevents their teen from later modifying the speed limit.

Industry observers note that the launch comes as part of the rebirth of Juiced Bikes following the brand’s acquisition last year. The firm was founded in 2009 and was acquired in 2025 by the co-founders of Lectric Ebikes, who have since brought the brand back with a upcoming generation of its popular Scrambler platform.

The biggest changes appear to be in the powertrain, battery, brakes, and suspension.

According to recent reports, the standard Scrambler Hardtail introduced earlier this year set the standard for the flagship models by using a 750W nominal motor with 90 Nm of torque and reaching 28 mph (45 km/h). Its 52V 19.2Ah battery provides nearly 1 kWh of capacity and a claimed range of up to 60 miles (96 km).

According to recent reports, the Scrambler Core steps down to a 500W nominal rear hub motor rated for 1,176W peak and 80 Nm of torque. Top speed is also reduced slightly to 25 mph (40 km/h), while the throttle is limited to 20 mph (32 km/h). Importantly, though, Juiced has retained its 52V architecture, meaning this is still a fairly punchy setup rather than a dramatically detuned budget bike.

Battery capacity takes a hit as well. The standard Core gets a 52V 10Ah battery with 520 Wh of capacity, rated for up to 40 miles (64 km) of range. Spending another $200 gets the Core Long-Range with a 52V 15Ah, 780Wh battery and a claimed 60-mile (96 km) maximum range. As with nearly all e-bikes, expect real-world range to fall short of the idealized advertised numbers, which are generally only achievable under the lowest power pedal assist.

Industry observers note that juiced also traded the Talon P4 four-piston hydraulic brakes found on the more expensive Scrambler for Talon P2 two-piston brakes. The KKE inverted fork with 140mm of travel is gone too, replaced by a more conventional aluminum triple-crown fork with 100mm of travel.

Those are meaningful downgrades, but they’re also largely the kinds of changes I’d expect to see when trying to shave $300 off an already competitively priced moto-style e-bike. It’s a strategy we’ve seen play out before in the industry, helping lower costs for riders who want a flagship bike but don’t necessarily want to pay flagship prices.

Sources indicate that even so, crucial features remain to help maintain the look and feel of the Juiced Scrambler line. The Core still gets 20 x 4-inch fat tires, hydraulic disc brakes, a frame-integrated TFT display, four pedal-assist levels, a headlight, taillight, brake light, and turn signals. It’s a single-speed setup and weighs 73 lb (33 kg), while being rated for a 300 lb (136 kg) payload.

Perhaps the more interesting addition is the Scrambler Core Midsize.

While the regular Core is recommended for riders 5’2” and taller, the Midsize drops that figure to just 4’10”. Pricing remains the same: $1,399 with the 520Wh battery or $1,599 with the 780Wh long-range pack.

And with an eye towards safety, the Core and Core Mini retain Juiced’s PIN-protected parental speed lock. Parents can set the motor-assisted top speed anywhere from 1-25 mph and lock the setting behind a four-digit PIN. That makes even more sense on the Midsize version, which seems tailor-made for younger riders who want the moto-style look but may not yet comfortably fit the larger Scrambler.

Industry observers note that the Core is launching in several decidedly Juiced color names, including Black Nectar, Fruit Punch, Sour Grape, White Grape, Berry Freeze, and Blood Orange, though availability varies between frame sizes and battery configurations. Juiced states preorders are expected to begin shipping around the end of the month.

At $1,399, the Scrambler Core feels like a logical extension of Juiced’s rebooted lineup. You lose some battery, motor power, braking hardware, suspension travel, and a few mph compared to the Hardtail, but the underlying recipe is largely intact. For riders who mostly want the Scrambler look and feel – or parents shopping for a smaller rider – saving $300 may be a pretty compelling trade. Especially when you consider that the original Juiced Scrambler already led the industry in value for moto-style e-bikes from reputable brands.

Toss in the strong backing from Lectric and the 3-year warranty, and it’s hard to consider much else among the competition.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The bitcoin price slumped under $62,000 on Thursday afternoon, according to Look Into Bitcoin data, extending a slide of about 24% in one month as Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut set off a broad selloff in tech stocks.

In a recent development, bitcoin was trading near $81,800 on Oct. 19. It touched a low of about $61,650 on Thursday, its weakest level since July, before steadying near $62,200. The drop was about 25% from the Oct. 19 close, based on daily data.

It has been revealed that the slide came in steps. Bitcoin closed near $80,050 on Oct. 25, about $78,250 on Nov. 1 and about $74,750 on Nov. 8. The steepest leg came last week, when it fell about 12.6% to a Nov. 15 close near $65,300, and the losses have continued this week.

Bitcoin had climbed back to about $64,000 early Thursday as Anthropic’s record IPO lifted stock futures, as this morning’s report showed. The rally faded once U.S. markets opened. The bitcoin price fell from roughly $63,900 at the opening bell to about $62,200 by midday.

It has been revealed that anthropic shares opened shortly before noon at $111.50, 34% above the $83 IPO price, CNBC reported. The opening trade valued the Claude maker at more than $2 trillion. The stock quickly pulled back and was last near $97, about 17% above its offering price.

It has been revealed that the broader market went the other way. The major averages fell to session lows soon after Anthropic began trading, as investors took profits on the AI trade. The Nasdaq Composite dropped about 2% after gaining as much as 2% earlier in the session, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost about 1,000 points.

According to recent reports, steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers, told CNBC the premarket rally had faded even before Anthropic began trading. He called it the latest round of “sell the rally” trading. Nvidia (NVDA) fell about 3%, and the S&P 500 headed toward a sixth straight loss, the AP reported.

According to recent reports, the Cboe Volatility Index, Wall Street’s fear gauge, climbed to about 28 after touching nearly 29 shortly after Anthropic began trading. That was its highest level since March, up from about 24.6 at Wednesday’s close. The bitcoin price moved in step with the Nasdaq through the afternoon.

Industry observers note that crypto stocks followed the Nasdaq lower in late-afternoon trading, about 3:55 p.m. ET. Strategy (MSTR) traded near $86.70, down about 4% on the day. Galaxy Digital (GLXY) dropped about 6.9%, the steepest decline in the group.

In a recent development, coinbase (COIN) slipped about 0.9% to near $109.50, while Circle (CRCL) fell about 2.2%. Bitcoin miners gave back their early rally too. IREN (IREN) fell about 5.6%, CleanSpark (CLSK) lost about 5.4% and MARA Holdings (MARA) declined about 4.2%. Riot Platforms (RIOT) was down about 2.9%.

The Fed remains a headwind. Bets on a December rate hike have grown after minutes from the October meeting revealed more policymakers backing higher rates, and some officials called for a half-point move.

According to recent reports, the bitcoin price is also on track for a seventh straight weekly loss, which would be its second-longest losing streak after nine weeks of declines in 2022. The streak has erased roughly $20,000 from the bitcoin price since mid-October, based on daily closes. Bitcoin price hit its weakest level since July on Thursday, and the Fed meets again next month.

It has been revealed that longer-term holders have not left. Institutional investors added 49,229 BTC through U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs in the third quarter, lifting their holdings to a record 356,491 BTC. Swiss bank Sygnum called the current downturn the shallowest bear market to date and sees a path to a fresh high near $128,000.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $61,900.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Air pollution from power plants supplying US data centers contributed to an estimated 650 premature deaths in 2023, researchers found.

An MIT-led study published Nov. 19 found that pollution associated with data center electricity demand traveled across state boundaries, exposing communities with relatively few facilities to elevated health risks.

The findings follow separate Harvard University research estimating that major US data centers generated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions over a 12-month period, highlighting the environmental costs accompanying the artificial intelligence industry's expansion.

The MIT researchers examined how data centers' electricity demand influenced power generation and air pollution across the contiguous United States in 2023.

Their findings, published in Environmental Research Letters, attributed 513 premature deaths to fine particulate pollution and another 137 to ground-level ozone.

Together, those deaths represented approximately 5.3% of the country's estimated mortality linked to electricity-related air pollution.

The 2023 model followed electricity demand across the grid and tracked how the resulting emissions moved through the air.

Sources indicate that contiguous US, 2023. The study estimated 513 premature deaths from fine particles and 137 from ground-level ozone.

Source: Environmental Research Letters · MIT CS3 study abstract · MIT News.

The place that draws the power and the place exposed to its pollution can be in different states.

Sources indicate that the diagram illustrates the study’s mechanism without mapping any single plant or route. The chart reveals modeled counts for 2023 grid electricity and excludes onsite backup generation.

In a recent development, the authors modeled hourly dispatch with and without 2023 data center load, then simulated air pollution and applied published exposure and mortality relationships. The chart demonstrates their reported estimates for the contiguous US.

The diagram illustrates the study’s mechanism without mapping any single plant or route. The chart indicates modeled counts for 2023 grid electricity and excludes onsite backup generation.

According to recent reports, virginia and Texas accounted for the largest data center electricity demand, consuming 33.9 and 21.8 terawatt-hours, respectively. However, Iowa, Nevada, South Dakota, and Kansas recorded some of the highest estimated death rates per resident, despite several having relatively few data centers.

The geographical imbalance reflects how America's interconnected electricity grid distributes the environmental consequences of growing power demand.

For example, electricity consumption by Virginia data centers can increase generation at coal and natural gas plants in the Ohio Valley. Emissions from those facilities subsequently travel through the atmosphere, where they can combine with ammonia from agricultural activities in the Midwest to form harmful fine particles.

These pollutants are associated with heart attacks, strokes, and respiratory illnesses.

The researchers also found that rural populations faced significantly higher estimated mortality risks than urban communities, extending the health consequences beyond the regions hosting major computing facilities.

The analysis tracked how power plants responded to data center electricity demand and used atmospheric models to estimate where the resulting pollution accumulated.

Recent findings suggest that A separate Harvard-led study published Nov. 16 in Nature Sustainability examined electricity consumption and carbon emissions across 403 major US data centers between May 2024 and April 2025.

The researchers estimated that the facilities consumed approximately 82 terawatt-hours of electricity, equivalent to 1.8% of total US electricity consumption.

That demand was associated with approximately 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions, with fossil fuels accounting for roughly 54% of the electricity generation attributed to the facilities.

Depending on assumptions about electricity demand, estimated emissions ranged from 21 million to 31 million metric tons.

The study also found that the facilities' average carbon intensity was approximately 314 grams of carbon dioxide per kilowatt-hour, compared with the national electricity generation average of 348 grams.

The Harvard findings add to concerns about the environmental costs of hyperscale computing infrastructure as technology companies expand capacity to meet growing demand for AI services.

While Harvard examined greenhouse gas emissions, MIT traced how electricity generation contributes to air pollution and premature mortality.

The findings intensify scrutiny of where new data centers are built and how their electricity is generated.

MIT researchers urged planners to consider air-quality consequences across affected regions, including communities far from the facilities, when deciding where to locate fresh computing infrastructure.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that the latest feature allows cyclists using a compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin smartwatch to share their location through Garmin’s LiveTrack feature.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Garmin and Waze are teaming up on an interesting new safety feature that could give cyclists a little extra protection when sharing the road with cars – by making cyclists themselves show up in Waze.

Sources indicate that the latest feature allows cyclists using a compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin smartwatch to share their location through Garmin’s LiveTrack feature. That location can then appear in real time to nearby drivers using Waze, with cyclists displayed as moving icons on the road.

As someone who recently joined the Garmin family myself with a smartwatch for tracking my cycling, running, and other activities, this is exactly the type of feature I love seeing added to the platform.

I’ve long maintained that safety – or more accurately, the perception that cycling isn’t safe – is one of the biggest impediments to getting more people onto bikes.

That’s especially true in the US, where cyclists are often forced to share roads with cars instead of enjoying the kind of widespread separated cycling infrastructure found in many more bike-friendly countries. And when a cyclist and a multi-ton vehicle have to occupy the same space, making sure the driver knows that cyclist is there can make a significant difference.

Of course, an icon on Waze isn’t going to magically make cycling safe. It won’t replace protected bike lanes, better road design, slower vehicle speeds, or attentive drivers.

According to recent reports, but I can certainly imagine situations where it could help. Riding at night or in poor visibility, approaching a blind curve, or simply traveling on a narrow road where a driver might otherwise come upon a cyclist unexpectedly are all situations where an advance warning could be useful.

Industry observers note that the feature is opt-in through Garmin Connect and activates when the cyclist starts an outdoor cycling activity. Garmin states location sharing is temporary and session-based, and that cyclists’ personal information isn’t displayed in Waze. Of course, anyone who uses a personal GPS device has already accepted that their location is shared with Substantial Tech in exchange for features they value, but at least we know that any personalized info stays within Garmin instead of proliferating even further.

Recent findings suggest that this is cool but requires both a Garmin product and the Waze app. IMHO better to equip new cars and trucks with bicycle and pedestrian detection.

Garmin LiveTrack itself is free for users with compatible Garmin devices and previously allowed cyclists to share their live location, speed, route, and other information with friends and family. I’ve used it myself as a safety feature when venturing off-road and on longer solo journeys. The Waze integration essentially expands that safety net to nearby motorists.

There’s obviously one major limitation: You need to be riding with a compatible Garmin device, and the driver needs to be using Waze.

But with Waze claiming around 200 million users globally and Garmin being one of the biggest names in cycling computers and fitness watches, that’s not exactly a tiny Venn diagram.

Anything that gives drivers another chance to see cyclists before actually seeing them sounds like a win to me.

7 Best Weighted Blankets to Sleep Better and Ease Anxiety, According to Editors

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • Weighted blankets are a force in the sleep world, with fans swearing they can do everything from easing anxiety to helping you sleep better.
  • According to recent reports, still, if you’ve spent any amount of time wrapped in a weighted blanket, you know how cozy it can feel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Weighted blankets are a force in the sleep world, with fans swearing they can do everything from easing anxiety to helping you sleep better. While there are some small studies to support those claims, the science is still catching up.

According to recent reports, still, if you’ve spent any amount of time wrapped in a weighted blanket, you know how cozy it can feel. You’re basically in a cocoon, protected from the outside world. That extra weight also means this blanket won’t just slide off during the night, keeping you nice and snug all night long.

Sources indicate that how do they work, you ask? The concept is pretty simple: These types of blankets mimic healing touch—something that reduces cortisol (the stress hormone) and boosts oxytocin (the feel-good hormone), Heidi Hanna, PhD, author of Stressaholic and an advisory board member for the American Institute of Stress, explains.

“While there isn’t much research to verify, the theory is that a weighted blanket works much like a hug,” adds Leisha Cuddihy, PhD, a clinical psychologist in behavioral sleep medicine. Hugging lowers blood pressure and stress hormones, which she indicates can help you snooze soundly. So, if you’re looking for some much-needed relief in the p.m., a weighted blanket is worth a try. Weighted blankets also make excellent holiday presents—who doesn’t want the gift of sleep?

Recent findings suggest that not all weighted blankets are created equal, though. Fill, material, and the actual weight of the blanket matter.

Industry observers note that the most Instagrammable beauty of the bunch, Bearaby’s chunky weighted blanket is hand-knitted with layers of responsibly farmed organic cotton. Plus, since it doesn’t have fillers that pack in warmth, you’ll stay cozy without melting into a sweaty puddle overnight.

WH social media editor Alyssa Cruz slept with this blanket for a month and claims it feels “just right” at night. “I absolutely love this blanket,” she shares, adding that the Bearaby blanket has improved her quality of sleep. “It is extremely comforting, and I find myself falling asleep within minutes,” she says. The blanket is so popular that Cruz and her roommate have taken turns sleeping with it. “The only cons is the size,” Cruz says. “You definitely have to be strategic with how you place it on your body, because it is very rectangular.” (Bearaby offers three different weights and sizes, giving you options to work with.) But Cruz says she’s still hooked. “I love it, and would buy ten more if I could.”.

In a recent development, make way for the OG. This weighted blanket made its debut in 2017, following the makers’ successful $5 million Kickstarter campaign to fund production. Gridded stitching on the blanket ensures that glass beads are distributed evenly, reaching every pressure point. Plus, we love the velvety flannel material for colder months.

According to recent reports, gravity has a smart design that makes this blanket easy to care for: Just remove the outside cover and toss it in the washing machine. (The inner blanket is hand wash only.) If you tend to run hot, this isn’t the blanket for you—it can get pretty toasty at night. But if you’re on the hunt for a snuggly weighted blanket that’s convenient and comfortable, give this one a go.

Recent findings suggest that weighted blankets tend to be pricey, with some costing upwards of $200. But the ZZZhen weighted blanket is just $30, making it accessible to most people. The blanket has a smooth exterior and internal grid system that’s designed to keep the interior glass beads in place.

According to recent reports, this blanket does the trick, delivering that classic warm hug feeling people crave in a weighted blanket. It’s also soft, and machine washable, making it easy to care for. We like that it comes in a 7-pound size, giving people new to weighted blankets a lighter-weight option if they want to ease in.

According to recent reports, of course, there are a few sacrifices to consider while you’re saving money. It’s unclear what the blanket is made from—some descriptions say cotton, while others say polyester. The sizing also tends to run a little small. But you can still get a lot for $30 with this option.

Recent findings suggest that weighted blankets take a little more thought than regular blankets. You have to figure out a weight that’s best for your needs, along with choosing a color that fits your decor. While many weighted blanket companies limit you to two or three weight options, YnM allows you to pick from 11 choices, along with 22 shades, giving you plenty of room for customization.

The blanket is made from a lightweight cotton for a surprisingly breezy feel. Available in weights from 7 to 50 pounds, the blanket is composed of seven layers that snugly envelop your every curve. But its largest size is 88” by 104”, allowing you to share it with a partner.

Available in three, eight, and 10-pound options, the Lola Weighted Blanket is great for anyone who wants some heft without feeling too heavy. The double-sided OEKO-TEX Standard 100-certified faux fur is unbelievably silky-soft, plus Its stain-resistant and sheds zero.

“It kept me warm and cozy without being overwhelming because of the extra weight,” claims WH social media producer Rianna Cafaro. “It was just right.” While some weighted blankets look utilitarian, that’s not the case with the Lola blanket. It’s fuzzy exterior makes it incredibly inviting. While Cafaro didn’t notice any drawbacks of this blanket during testing, she did point out that it’s pricey. Still, she says, “it is worth the price.”.

Straying from the pack, Layla’s blanket is available in only one weight, depending on your mattress size. But that means it’s enough for you and your bedmate to share (score!). The top layer is plush, while the other feels like a cool cotton bedsheet.

WH fitness and reviews editor Natascha Grief loved the fabric options, especially the plush side. “It kind of feels like being hugged by a stuffed animal,” she indicates. Grief says that the blanket delivers a comforting feel without the bulk. “The fill was silent and virtually unnoticeable,” she says. “It didn't shift around every time I did.” Grief also says she didn’t notice any uncomfortable pressure points like she has in the past as a side sleeper with other weighted blankets.

The only downside, per Grief, is that this only comes in one color (black). While you can toss the whole thing in the wash, just be aware of your machine’s capacity. Larger sizes may be tough to stuff into a compact washer.

There’s a wide range of textures with weighted blankets—some have a stuffed animal-like feel, while others are more functional. The Baloo weighted blanket falls into the second camp, with a comforter style design you can toss on your bed and leave there.

Recent findings suggest that WH entertainment editor Amy Wilkinson praises the temperature regulation of this blanket, noting that it felt just right. It’s on the thinner side, but is great for layering and all-season use, she points out—just add on another layer in the winter and take one off in the summer. “The 15-pound weight felt just right for getting the soothing compression of a weighted blanket without feeling like you’re being squished in your sleep,” Wilkinson states. Just be aware that you may need to size up. Wilkinson got a full/queen size and found that it didn’t cover her entire queen bed. Still, she says, “as a no-frills comforter, it does the job.”.

It’s no surprise that this is the most crucial consideration. There’s no one perfect weight. Rather, it’s essential to get a blanket that’s right for your body type. Weighted blankets typically range from 5 to 30 pounds, and many experts suggest picking one that’s around 10 percent of your body weight. This will ensure you don’t experience any discomfort as you sleep. Ideally, you want the right amount of pressure without putting so much weight on your body that you feel “trapped” or suffocated.

Recent findings suggest that you’ll want a blanket that offers uniform pressure to feel the calming effect, says Cuddihy. Look for quality stitching, layers of material, and glass-bead fill. Some lower-quality weighted blankets will have plastic pellets instead of glass beads, so keep an eye out when shopping.

Recent findings suggest that depending on the time of year and whether you run hot or cold, the material your weighted blanket is made from matters. If you’re a hot sleeper, look for blankets made with breathable fabrics like bamboo or cotton. A removable cover can be helpful, too, for easier machine washing. If you like to be bundled in warmth under your blankets, look for materials like fleece or microfiber.

Weighted blankets need to be washed, too, making it important to find one that won’t make your life harder. Blankets filled with glass microbeads, plastic pellets, steel beads, or pebbles can usually go in the wash, while those that are filled with organic materials often can’t. Your washing machine may also not be able to handle the extra weight. So, read the care instructions before purchasing your blanket to make sure it lines up with your lifestyle.

There’s a lot of variety with weighted blanket sizing, making it key to read the measurements carefully. If you strategy to use your weighted blanket on your bed like a comforter, or just want to make sure it’ll cover your body while you snooze, try measuring out the size on your bed to see what it will look like to get a better sense. Consider sizing up if you’re unsure.

Our editors regularly test bedding, including weighted blankets, and they continue to try latest products as they’re released. We last updated this story in March. Since then, we tested four additional weighted blankets for a month or more.

Industry observers note that we spent many nights at home snuggled under weighted blankets comparing weight, texture, temperature regulation, size, and performance. Naturally, comfort was heavily weighed during testing. When testing, we also took into consideration which blankets were best for the sofa versus for actually sleeping under for the night.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even in the age of one-click shopping, opening an actual brick-and-mortar retail store is a dream for many designers. There’s something almost romantic about creating an entire environment where customers can sit on the sofas, feel the fabrics, or pick up a last-minute gift on their way to a party. It’s an opportunity to bring your brand to life and connect with customers in a way a website never can.

But opening a store requires a significant leap of faith. Even if you have a loyal customer base, there’s something different about building a store. You have to think about everything from foot traffic to merchandising to hiring staff, and much more.

Sources indicate that these are questions I’ve been wrestling with myself. Almost two months ago, after years of nurturing a thriving e-commerce business, my husband Syd and I unveiled our McGee & Co. flagship in our homebase of Salt Lake City. This project has been a goal of ours for a long time. We’ve been collecting ideas for years to ensure that whenever it opened, our physical retail operation would hold up to the high standards of service and design that we expect from every other part of our business. This project has had me thinking about retail at every hour of the day, mulling over some significant questions... How do we translate a digital brand into a physical space for selling? How do we nurture customers and ensure they return? And how do we map our knowledge so that we can repeat our successes as we scale?

In a recent development, this guide, produced with our friends at AD PRO, distills some of the wisdom from our own experiences, as well as from a few insiders elsewhere in the industry. I’ll share some of the thinking and practical decisions behind our shop, from our merchandising strategy to how we recruited and trained our employees.

Next, AD PRO contributor Lila Allen speaks to me and my team, as well as professionals from retailers like Lawson-Fenning, Il Buco Vita, Tailor-Made Textiles, and ABC Carpet & Home, about how they cultivate customer loyalty over the long term. When access to product and knowledge is seemingly unlimited across the internet, we all agree: Earning trust and becoming a destination for discovery takes a lot of care. But it pays off. Relationships might be the most precious resource we have.

Then, contributor Margaret Borden catches up with the creatives behind some of this year’s buzziest shops—from a jewel-box fashion boutique in Paris to a bright, inviting kitchen and home goods shop in New York City—to glean their merchandising tips and tricks.

Whether you’re a designer thinking about hanging your own retail shingle, or you’re simply looking for a fresh perspective on the landscape of selling in 2026 and beyond, I hope this report will give you plenty of inspiration for the year ahead.

Our Salt Lake City flagship is a baptism by fire—but we wouldn’t have it any other way. Here’s how we planned our first retail location for profitability, growth, and an unmistakably “McGee” experience —As Told to Lila Allen.

According to recent reports, in the age of instant gratification and easy comparison shopping, relationships matter more than ever. Here’s how retail pros across the country are building them—and keeping them —By Lila Allen.

Sources indicate that how do you design a store enticing enough to lure people off their sofas and through the door? The creatives behind four of 2026’s buzziest shops reveal their strategies —By Margaret Borden.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Who indicates long EV road trips mean hours at charging stations? BMW drove the latest i3 for over 3 days, covering nearly 3,700 miles, and it took less than 3 hours of charging.

BMW put the i3 to the ultimate test of efficiency, charging speed, and long-distance EV capability on a nearly 3,700-mile Pan-European journey.

In a recent development, the Paneurpeana, as it’s called, is considered the benchmark for range and charging speed. The route begins at the North Cape in Norway, the northernmost point of continental Europe you can reach by car, and ends in Tarifa, Spain, the southernmost point of mainland Europe.

BMW drove the fresh i3 50 xDrive for a total of 3,658 miles (5,886.7 km) across eight countries and spent just 2 hours, 45 minutes, and 54 seconds charging at an average of 275 kW.

The performance beat the previous record by more than seven hours, according to Mike Reichelt, head of BMW’s Neue Klasse.

BMW noted the charging points were not predetermined and that it had to account for external factors such as weather and traffic jams.

The upcoming i3 was impressively efficient during the trip, consuming an average of just 12.5 kWh per 100 km, beating its official WLTP combined energy consumption of 18-13.4 kWh/100 km.

BMW stated the trip took 3 days, 2 hours, and 41 minutes, with an average speed of 79.7 km/h, and that the i3 was charged exclusively at public charging points across national charging networks.

The vehicle was driven at all times by a single driver and was not modified in any way, in terms of hardware or software, from the standard i3 available for purchase.

BMW’s new i3 uses a 108.7 kWh battery and Gen6 eDrive system that provides a WLTP range of up to 566 miles (912 km).

With a drag coefficient of just 0.21, the latest i3 is the most aerodynamically efficient BMW vehicle to date.

In the US, BMW noted the new 2027 i3 50 xDrive will offer an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 468 miles.

According to recent reports, with an 800V architecture, the electric sedan can add nearly 262 miles (423 km) of range (WLTP) in about 10 minutes at DC fast-charging speeds up to 400 kW. In the US, the i3 has a built-in NACS port.

In a recent development, very reasonable. I've been with NK iX3 from Spain to Estonia and the experience is real - low consumption, great comfort and really fast charging. And there are more and more high speed chargers every month.

Recent findings suggest that like the new iX3, the i3 features BMW’s Neue Klasse interior design. The setup consists of BMW’s massive 43″ Panoramic Vision display that spans the base of the windshield and a 17.9″ floating central infotainment display.

The upcoming BMW i3 50 xDrive is on sale in Germany starting at €65,900 with a WLTP range of up to 566 miles (912 km).

In the US, the 2027 BMW i3 50 xDrive and 2027 iX3 50 xDrive are available to order, both starting at $61,500.
