#6080. QuantumScape unveils Osprey all-solid-state cell: 1,000 cycles at 1 atm

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1600 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

QuantumScape unveils Osprey all-solid-state cell: 1,000 cycles at 1 atm

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1600 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that quantumScape (QS) is finally going all-solid-state.
  • That’s a substantial deal for the sulfide camp, which includes Toyota, Samsung SDI, BYD, and Factorial.
  • Here’s something QuantumScape has rarely spelled out this plainly: its current product isn’t all-solid-state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that quantumScape (QS) is finally going all-solid-state. Its newly introduced Osprey platform swaps the liquid in its cathode for a sulfide solid electrolyte, and the company says the cells have hit 1,000 full cycles to 80% capacity at just one atmosphere of pressure.

That’s a substantial deal for the sulfide camp, which includes Toyota, Samsung SDI, BYD, and Factorial. Their cells typically need heavy clamping to work. But the white paper behind the announcement shows these are small, early lab cells, and some headline numbers come with notable conditions.

Here’s something QuantumScape has rarely spelled out this plainly: its current product isn’t all-solid-state.

The upcoming white paper describes the QSE platform, including the QSE-5 cell it’s shipping as samples from its Eagle Line pilot production in San Jose, as a ceramic separator paired with “a relatively conventional high-nickel NMC cathode and a liquid catholyte.”.

The solid part is the separator. It sits between the cathode and a lithium-metal anode that QuantumScape doesn’t manufacture at all. The cell is built “anode-free,” and lithium plates against the separator during the first charge.

Osprey keeps that separator and anode-free design and swaps the liquid in the cathode for a solid sulfide electrolyte. That makes the whole cell solid.

It has been revealed that the interesting part is that QuantumScape hasn’t changed its mind on sulfides. It has spent years arguing that sulfide electrolytes can’t work as separators, and the white paper doubles down, calling their problems “fundamental properties” of the material rather than engineering challenges.

The company lists four problems: sulfides react with lithium metal, they need high pressure to keep contact with the electrodes, they struggle at room temperature and below, and they can’t handle fast charging with a lithium-metal anode before dendrites form.

It has been revealed that the pressure point is the one automakers care about most. QuantumScape illustrates it this way: 20 atm on a single 10 x 24.2 cm cell works out to roughly 5,000 kg of force, about three mid-size cars. Holding that across a pack takes thick steel end plates and tie rods, which add weight, volume, and cost.

Recent findings suggest that and 20 atm is on the generous side. Many sulfide cells in labs run at 30 to 100+ atm (3 to 12 MPa), and some even higher. China’s FAW reported large-format sulfide cells cycling at 5 MPa, or about 50 atm, in September, which was billed as a low-pressure achievement.

So QS’s pitch is simple: keep the sulfide in the cathode, where it’s good at moving lithium ions, and let the QS ceramic separator handle the lithium metal.

QuantumScape published four main data sets:.

According to recent reports, this is the strongest result. A 2-layer cell with a 50 x 65 mm cathode, the same area as QSE-5, ran 1,000 cycles to about 80% capacity. The test used full 1C charge and 1C discharge, 0 to 100% state of charge, 30°C, and 1 atm. The cathode loading was 5.5 mAh/cm², which is in line with commercial EV cells.

According to recent reports, quantumScape states no other sulfide-based cell has shown this, and Electrek couldn’t find published data that contradicts it. Academic groups have shown sulfide cells running with little or no external pressure, but not for 1,000 full cycles with a sulfide cathode and lithium-metal anode.

But this is a small cell. By our math, two layers at that size come out to roughly 0.3 to 0.4 Ah, compared to about 5 Ah for a QSE-5.

The press release claims “five-minute fast charging from 10% to 80%.” The white paper demonstrates that was achieved at 10C, in a 2-layer cell, at 80°C (176°F). The chart itself is captioned “High temperature enables 5 min fast charge.”.

Industry observers note that batteries charge much faster when hot, and EVs do precondition packs before fast charging. Still, 80°C is well above what EV packs are usually preconditioned to before a fast charge. QS didn’t publish a room-temperature fast-charge result.

Industry observers note that “Operational down to -20°C” came from a single-layer cell with a 21 x 21 mm cathode, discharged slowly at C/3. It kept 68% of its room-temperature capacity at -20°C (about 52% of its energy) and 85% at 0°C.

According to recent reports, that’s a real result for a sulfide system, which have historically needed heat. But it’s a tiny cell at a gentle rate.

The “up to ~1,100 Wh/L” figure is a projection. QS indicates high-loading cathodes (10 mAh/cm², about double today’s EV cells) are possible with sulfide catholytes. The test backing that up used an 11 mm coin-size cell at 3 atm, not 1 atm, and ran for 100 cycles.

For reference, QSE-5 is rated at 844 Wh/L and 301 Wh/kg.

The business model is the bigger story.

It has been revealed that quantumScape is pitching Osprey as an “open platform.” Customers can use QS’s own sulfide cathode, made with a proprietary dry process, or bring their own. QS states it has already tested Osprey with solid cathodes developed by its automotive customers.

In other words, after years of being the sulfide skeptic, QuantumScape now wants to sell its separator and anode-free design to the companies that have spent billions developing sulfide cathodes.

Recent findings suggest that that fits the licensing model it already uses with Volkswagen’s PowerCo and Honda. QS reported $9.8 million in customer billings in Q3 and revealed a 100 MWh production line targeting start of production in 2028 for QSE-5.

According to recent reports, there’s no timeline for Osprey. The white paper says the process has been demonstrated “at laboratory scale,” that higher-throughput processes are “in the development stage,” and that “significant work remains in process engineering.” Automakers also want larger prismatic cells than QSE-5, which means more layers and more area per layer.

Everyone else is on the clock. Samsung SDI is targeting mass production of sulfide all-solid-state cells in its Ulsan plant in the second half of 2027. BYD aims small-batch sulfide solid-state production in 2027, with mass production toward the end of the decade. Toyota is aiming for 2027 to 2028, after slipping from 2020, 2023, and 2026. Factorial’s sulfide Solstice platform is targeting up to 450 Wh/kg.

CATL, the world’s largest battery maker, stated in June that true mass-market solid-state is still “years away,” around 2030.

In a recent development, none of those companies has published 1,000-cycle data at 1 atm with a sulfide cathode and lithium-metal anode. That’s QuantumScape’s opening shot.

This is the most interesting thing QuantumScape has published in a while. The numbers are good, but the strategy shift probably stands out most.

The cycle-life result is legit. A 2-layer cell with commercial-area electrodes and realistic loading doing 1,000 full 1C cycles at 1 atm and 30°C is the kind of data the industry hasn’t shown. And QS published the test conditions, which is more than many of its competitors do.

Key thing to remember is that this is a lab test cell. There's a long road ahead to mass manufacturing.

According to recent reports, also, when it hopefully hits the market it will be an incremental improvement, not a quantum leap. Current cells are already in the market doing things like 5 minute charging.

But you can argue the press release oversells what’s in the white paper. A 5-minute charge at 80°C isn’t the same thing as a 5-minute charge, and the release should have said so. The energy density is projected, the cold-weather result is from a cell the size of a postage stamp, and 80% after 1,000 cycles is well below the 95% after 1,000 cycles PowerCo confirmed in QSE’s early cells back in 2024. Different chemistry, different stage, but something worth keeping in mind.

It has been revealed that so QuantumScape is essentially admitting the liquid catholyte in QSE isn’t the end game, and that the industry’s massive sulfide investment is something to plug into rather than fight. If your separator is the one part everyone else can’t make work, selling it to them is smart.

It has been revealed that the question is time. QS is still scaling QSE-5, with a 100 MWh line not due until 2028. Osprey is a lab process. Will anyone in the sulfide camp license it before their own 2027 to 2030 production looks lock in? At this point, it sounds like this is QS’ bet right now.

#6075. Block Notes Most Bitcoin Payments on Square Are for Coffee and Food

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (637 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bitcoinmagazine ↗ Open Full Page

Block Notes Most Bitcoin Payments on Square Are for Coffee and Food

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (637 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most bitcoin payments at Square sellers are small, everyday purchases at coffee shops and restaurants, Block mentioned in a fresh report that it hopes will inform a debate in Congress over a tax break for small crypto purchases.
  • The report, “The State of Bitcoin Payments,” covers completed bitcoin payments at U.S.
  • Recent findings suggest that food and drink businesses took 72% of those payments, Block found.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most bitcoin payments at Square sellers are small, everyday purchases at coffee shops and restaurants, Block mentioned in a fresh report that it hopes will inform a debate in Congress over a tax break for small crypto purchases.

The report, “The State of Bitcoin Payments,” covers completed bitcoin payments at U.S. Square sellers from Nov. 1, 2025, to Oct. 15, 2026. The median payment was about $13, and the average was about $29.

Recent findings suggest that food and drink businesses took 72% of those payments, Block found. That is a bigger share than the category’s 67.5% slice of regular card payments on Square over the same period.

“Most bitcoin payments are small and routine,” the firm wrote on X Thursday, calling the report one of the first datasets on how people spend bitcoin in the local economy.

Coffee shops and fast food businesses accounted for 62.6% of the bitcoin payments in the food and drink category, with a median payment of $9.10. Grocery stores made up a smaller share but had the highest average payment in the group, at $60.73.

Small tickets dominated. About 42% of bitcoin payments on Square were under $10, and 65.1% were under $20. Those sub-$20 payments made up just 19.1% of total payment value, though, with a few larger purchases accounting for much of the dollars spent.

According to recent reports, customers also came back. Among Cash App users who paid with bitcoin at least twice at the same merchant, the median was three purchases per customer-merchant pair. About 44% of bitcoin payments from Cash App were repeat payments, and 86% of those came within 30 days.

The activity was not limited to Block’s own app. External Lightning wallets such as Strike, Wallet of Satoshi, Phoenix and Coinbase handled 56.6% of Square bitcoin payments and about 66% of payment value, while Cash App wallets made up the rest.

According to recent reports, square sellers can choose how much of each sale they keep in bitcoin, and Square converts the rest to dollars automatically. Block remarked zero-fee processing for bitcoin payments on Square has been extended through Dec. 31, 2027. Local governments are testing similar setups, with Miami-Dade County now taking bitcoin for property taxes and converting it to dollars.

Block tied the data to tax policy. Under current U.S. federal rules, paying with bitcoin generally means calculating a capital gain or loss on every purchase, even a $10 coffee, the company noted.

Sources indicate that A Morning Consult survey that Block commissioned found that 23.6% of businesses that don’t accept bitcoin cite tax and accounting complexity as a reason. That is about the same share that cite regulation, refunds or price swings. Among businesses that have considered taking bitcoin but haven’t, the figure was 27%.

Recent findings suggest that consumers pointed to friction, too. Morning Consult surveyed 8,669 U.S. adults who are aware of bitcoin in August. Among those who don’t own it, 29.6% noted they would be more likely to pay with bitcoin if it were easier, and 15.7% of that group said they were unsure how it is taxed or regulated.

It has been revealed that block remarked Congress is weighing a crypto tax package and pointed to a de minimis exemption, which would exempt small gains on qualifying purchases, as one option. Industry groups have pressed lawmakers on crypto tax rules for months, with little movement so far.

The report doesn’t give totals. Block said the number of Square bitcoin payments, the number of sellers receiving them and total bitcoin payment volume are proprietary and not disclosed. Merchant lists like the 425 Los Angeles businesses that accept bitcoin offer a rough sense of reach.

“We think tax policy should account for how people spend bitcoin as well as how they hold it,” Block said.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, genesis opened orders for the ultra-luxury electric SUV in South Korea, with prices starting at over $100,000.
  • Hyundai’s luxury brand is moving upscale with the GV90, its first fully electric three-row flagship SUV.
  • After unveiling the GV90 at the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco in August (which we had the pleasure to see firsthand), Genesis launched the new “ultra-luxe” SUV in its home market of Korea on Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, genesis opened orders for the ultra-luxury electric SUV in South Korea, with prices starting at over $100,000. If you want coach doors, however, it will cost you a bit more.

Hyundai’s luxury brand is moving upscale with the GV90, its first fully electric three-row flagship SUV.

After unveiling the GV90 at the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco in August (which we had the pleasure to see firsthand), Genesis launched the new “ultra-luxe” SUV in its home market of Korea on Tuesday.

The Genesis GV90 introduces several “world-first” innovations, including the first independently opening and closing B-pillarless coach doors, a 12-airbag roof airbag system, and genuine wood floors with radiant heating.

It’s available in two models: the GV90 Standard with traditional swing doors and the GV90 Neolun, which features the “Neolun Arch Gate,” Genesis’ hidden B-pillar coach door system.

In Korea, the Genesis GV90 Standard 7-seater model starts at 139.5 million won, or about $104,000.

The GV90 Individual Lounge Seat (6-seater) starts at 145.5 million won ($108,500); the GV90 Neolun Standard (6-seater) starts at 189.9 million won ($141,500), while the top-spec GV90 Neolun Executive Suite (4-seater) starts at 239.5 million won ($178,500).

Based on Hyundai’s latest eMP platform, developed exclusively for its flagships, Genesis mentioned the GV90 is like a “moving private lounge,” complete with a multi-chamber air suspension and a dual electronic limited-slip differential (E-LSD).

The platform is designed to open up interior space for the B-pillarless coach doors, swivel seats, and more.

When parked, the front seats swivel a full 180 degrees to face rear passengers or to create what Genesis calls “a face-to-face lounge-like configuration.”.

The interior is about as over-the-top as you could expect, with massive digital screens, premium materials, and plenty of luxury extras.

The GV90 is the first Hyundai Motor Group vehicle to feature its new extendable display and the first Genesis model equipped with its next-gen Pleos Connect infotainment system.

Together, they create what Genesis calls a newly introduced realm of “display expandability.” While other vehicles, like the new Tucson and IONIQ 3, also use Pleos Connect, Hyundai developed an exclusive version for the GV90.

When the vehicle is parked, the screen can expand to 24.6″ at the push of a button, transforming it into a massive Cinematic Display.

Once extended, the display switches to Media Home mode, where you can watch Netflix, live TV, stream music, and more with third-party apps.

It has been revealed that A mobile private theater wouldn’t be complete without a premium audio system, right? To top it off, Genesis added a 25-speaker Bang & Olufsen Premier 3D Sound System with Dolby Atmos, so it sounds like you’re actually at the movies.

In place of a traditional instrument cluster, the GV90 has a 25″ Head-Up Display (HUD) that shows the vehicle’s speed, navigation directions, and other ADAS functions directly on the windshield.

According to recent reports, the GV90 is also the first Hyundai Motor Group vehicle with a buttonless power system. When you enter the vehicle and close the door, the Motion Column Shifter moves from the 12 o’clock position to the 2 o’clock position.

Meanwhile, the Crystal Sphere between the driver and passenger rotates to indicate it’s ready to drive. The vehicle starts when you press the brake.

As a full-size flagship SUV, the Genesis GV90 is massive. It measures 208.1″ (5,285 mm) long, 79.9″ (2,030 mm) wide, and 71.5″ (1,815 mm) tall (71.4″ with 24″ tires), with a 127.8″ (3,245 mm) wheelbase.

That’s even bigger than the Hyundai IONIQ 9 (199.2″/5,060 mm in length) and Kia EV9 (197.4″/5,010 mm).

Industry observers note that to power a full-size flagship SUV, it needs a major battery. The GV90 uses a 123.5 kWh battery, the largest among Hyundai Motor’s EVs, which Genesis said provides a driving range of 500 km (310 miles) for the 7-seater version with 22″ wheels.

The GV90 Neonlun 6-seater with 24″ wheels has a range of up to 460 km (286 miles) on a single charge.

It’s equipped with a new dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) system that delivers a combined 657 hp (490 kW) and 590 lb-ft (800 Nm) of torque, making it Hyundai Motor Group’s most powerful electric vehicle.

When using a 350 kW fast charger, the vehicle’s battery can recharge from 10% to 80% in about 22 minutes.

It has been revealed that and.... once again Hyundai shortchanges the range. If you are going to drop a 200+ inch premium upright SUV into the market it requires a 140+ kwh battery (Rivian, BMW) to deliver segment appropriate range. You do not have to jump to a 200 kwh Escalade (though it is probably a better buy in every respect) but at least deliver 140+. Also, memo to powertrain engineering group: 350 kw is getting outdated on fast charging especially on a vehicle of this size. And while I am at it, what happened to the promised L3 ADAS? I think the 2028 Caddy is worth the wait compared to this.

“Thanks to the enthusiastic interest and support for the GV90 since its global premiere, we have begun full-scale sales in Korea first,” a Genesis official stated, adding the flagship SUV will “set a newly introduced standard for luxury.”.

Following Korea, Genesis is expected to launch the GV90 in the US and other global markets in early 2027.

According to recent reports, genesis has yet to reveal US prices, but the GV90 Standard model is expected to start at around $100,000. The GV90 Neolun, on the other hand, will likely start closer to $150,000 or more.

According to recent reports, what do you think of the flagship Genesis GV90? Would you buy the standard version for about $100,000 or pay the extra for the Neolun with coach doors? Let us know in the comments.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even if you order takeout (almost) every evening, the best dining tables can make all of the difference for elevating your dishes, down to the cold leftovers you’ve reheated for dinner.
  • Ahead, we’re highlighting our 11 favorites, from a perfectly mod pedestal to an extendable farmhouse beauty.
  • Paired with the Meja dining chairs, Article’s Plumas table helped senior shopping editor Nashia Baker convert an empty living room nook into a dining setup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even if you order takeout (almost) every evening, the best dining tables can make all of the difference for elevating your dishes, down to the cold leftovers you’ve reheated for dinner. You don’t have to be a regular hostess to know that these furniture pieces are more than a place to eat; they double as a surface to display your latest tableware finds, function as a desk, and even help facilitate conversation. Whether you’re looking to outfit a quaint breakfast nook or source something with panache for a formal dining area, the best dining tables bring in just the right amount of personality without distracting from what’s actually key—the people you’re eating with.

Ahead, we’re highlighting our 11 favorites, from a perfectly mod pedestal to an extendable farmhouse beauty. Looking for a dining table that was made for small spaces? We have options for you too.

Paired with the Meja dining chairs, Article’s Plumas table helped senior shopping editor Nashia Baker convert an empty living room nook into a dining setup. With slightly angular legs and rounded corners, the table evokes a classic, midcentury silhouette (fitting perfectly with the rest of Baker’s apartment aesthetic). The extendable feature is accessible simply by pulling a latch underneath the table and sliding either end apart. With the table pushed against the wall, she states her “current setup works just fine to comfortably seat three people.” Baker does blueprint on using the extendable design during larger holiday parties “so there’s plenty of space for a potluck-style tablescape.”.

In a recent development, west Elm’s Miles dining table was the investment shopping producer Lauren Arzbaecher needed to fully maximize guest seating in her Brooklyn apartment. “I love playing host—poker nights, RuPaul’s Drag Race watch parties, you name it. An extendable table was an ideal solution to seat extra guests for a dinner party while not eating up extra square footage on a regular day,” she says. In the 60 to 80” size, Arzbaecher can sit up to 10 guests around the table (though it requires some squishing onto the matching bench). With a modern, rounded silhouette, the double-edge detailing along the sides of the tabletop perfectly complements the equally curvy dining chairs the producer already owned. And despite its substantial appearance, the table is surprisingly agile. “Don’t let the chunky look deceive you,” she says. “This table isn’t heavy, and I’ve been able to move the leaf in and out on my own with ease.”.

With a vibe that falls somewhere along the spectrum of an upstate farmhouse and Spanish revival, this rectangular dining table from Green Row charmed commerce writer Julia Harrison with its extendable surface and rich wood stain. “This table does the work of modern design at its best: It looks completely authentic—like it was lifted from a small rural French farm, dusted off, and dropped in my dining room in Brooklyn,” she notes. Extended, she notes that it comfortably fits eight people, and has paired it with some dark wood Windsor chairs to create an overall farmhouse-esque effect. “It's the sort of table that makes you want to host things, the way good writing can inspire you to write,” she adds.

Strikingly modern and architectural, the Aava dining table from Wayfair is the ideal budget pick for those still looking to make a major design impact. The perpendicular legs create a kind of futuristic aesthetic while the classic wood stain options (black, natural, and white) mean that this table can suit a number of design styles, from modern to minimal.

Recent findings suggest that pedestal tables boast timeless design appeal thanks to their streamlined build and versatile aesthetic (it’s part mod, part midcentury, part Scandi—this table fits anywhere). Architect Eero Saarinen was inspired to eliminate cumbersome legs from dining tables, and in doing so, he inspired countless dupes and recreations of his innovative round pedestal shape. Whether it’s just you in your apartment or a Thanksgiving-level gathering, this oval dining table offers a number of sizes to accommodate your friends and family. The sturdy, oval pedestal base ensures no drinks are spilled as you maneuver in and out of your seat, while the thin tabletop leaves ample room for all chair heights and seat positions.

For small apartment dwellers or those looking to finally stop eating meals on the couch, a space-saving bistro table is the way to go. This painted steel version from Schoolhouse, similar to a traditional pedestal dining table, is both durable and lightweight, offering plenty of room for a meal for two. The high-gloss finish is a dramatic (and welcome) reprieve from the traditional wood surfaces that characterize the genre.

Great for small dining spaces and eat-in kitchens, a drop-leaf silhouette offers a kind of versatility not seen in traditional dining tables. This best-seller from Pottery Barn has a rectangular frame with two sections that lower to create a smaller square for everyday use. The leaves also include additional supports that can lock into place for added stability.

In a recent development, it’s rare to find a stylish drop-leaf table, especially for those looking for a round option for their small dining area. This one from West Elm can collapse both sides to sit flush with the wall and save valuable floor space in small apartments (even the legs fold in). Extend one side only if it’s just you, or sit four dining chairs comfortably with a 42-inch diameter at full size.

Designed by fashion content creator Aimee Song, the Hannu round dining room table boasts a playful, bulbous shape. Made from fibercement (meaning it’s safe for both indoor and outdoor use), this table’s ivory finish and curved edges intentionally soften the materials' typically utilitarian applications.

In a recent development, sculptural and dramatic, this marble dining table holds its own against any number of statement seating choices. The black and white veining gives off an Italian modernist feeling, but this table can easily shift between design styles depending on what you choose to pair it with.

As seen in the Hollywood Hills home of TV writer and producer Cameron Johnson, this CB2 dining table has a streamlined, Brutalist feel with its offset legs. This solid wood dining table is available in both 63 inches (best for seating four to six) and 91 inches (best for six to eight seats).

Can Testosterone Add Inches to Your Penis?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Welcome to Testosterone HQ—Men's Health's guide to the exciting, complicated, and revolutionary world of testosterone.
  • IF TESTOSTERONE HELPS increase your penis size during puberty, surely taking TRT will help you get a bigger package?
  • Unfortunately, testosterone works a bit differently once you’re out of your late teens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Testosterone HQ—Men's Health's guide to the exciting, complicated, and revolutionary world of testosterone. For everything you need to know about T, click here.

IF TESTOSTERONE HELPS increase your penis size during puberty, surely taking TRT will help you get a bigger package?

Unfortunately, testosterone works a bit differently once you’re out of your late teens. Here’s what to know about that.

It has been revealed that testosterone, which is produced by your testicles, “plays a key role in the development of characteristics like libido, and growth of the penis and testicles,” states Jamin Brahmbhatt, MD, urologist at Orlando Health. The hormone surges in your body during your tween and teen years to achieve all of these changes (along with deepening of the voice, facial hair, and so on).

According to recent reports, the “blast” of testosterone is usually over by your mid- to late teens. Reproductive urologist Paul Turek, MD, says this is because fertility is achieved as the testicles and penis reach adult size.

YOUR PENIS DOES go through some interesting changes as you age, but it doesn’t get bigger.

It has been revealed that after testosterone stops surging in your late teens, your sexual development is set for life. Genetics are the main reason your penis grows to its permanent size. “You’re born with the size already determined,” says Dr. Brahmbhatt.

Sources indicate that now testosterone is still being produced in your body when you’re an adult, but it won’t have any further effect on penis size. That biological fact holds true no matter your penis length. One study done by researchers at the University of Utah School of Medicine found that stretched penile length did not have any association with testosterone levels in adult men.

Since the penis consists of spongy tissue, not muscle, there’s no way to build it up on your own. “There are no safe and effective methods for permanently increasing penis size,” states Dr. Brahmbhatt. Penis pumps might help with stronger erections, but they do nothing for overall size.

WHILE TESTOSTERONE HAD an effect on your penis length early on, more won't help now. It might even hurt to take any sketchy T boosters or penis enlargement pills that promise to increase your girth or length. You have no idea whether they’re safe to take or whether they contain harmful ingredients.

Industry observers note that A Stanford University study found that the average erect penile length has grown 24 percent worldwide over the past 29 years. The researchers report this is not due to an increase in testosterone levels.

Industry observers note that any change in development in a short amount of time is concerning. One of the authors of the study noted that chemical exposure could be interacting with the hormone makeup of guys—which may also explain lower sperm counts, increases in testicular cancer rates, and lower T levels in men nowadays.

In a recent development, the bottom line is that size doesn’t matter. Your penis health—especially function—does. If you notice any changes in how your penis looks or functions—patchy spots, bumps, curves—definitely don’t ignore them.

And while it’s natural to be curious about how your penis stacks up with other guys, don’t worry. The average penis length is not as massive as you think.

She is the author of eight best-selling books, including The Essentials of Theater.

#6062. Tech Report: Michelle Yeoh on Strength, Stunts, and What Makes Us Human

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2244 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Michelle Yeoh on Strength, Stunts, and What Makes Us Human

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2244 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, an action hero used to have to be massive and brawny and brusque.
  • Starring as Olwen, a bioengineered artificial human (or “replicant,” as they’re called in the Blade Runner universe, which includes the upcoming series Blade Runner 2099, out November 25 on Amazon Prime Video), the 64-year-old global megastar literally wrestles with people and replicants alike on-screen.
  • Sources indicate that but in real life, she dances with even larger issues.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, an action hero used to have to be massive and brawny and brusque. Michelle Yeoh is none of those things—but you feel her presence and power the instant you meet her. She is kind, warm, and lovely, but she’s also intense…in a really good way. This is a person who listens closely yet also seems ready to launch into a wheelhouse kick at any moment.

Starring as Olwen, a bioengineered artificial human (or “replicant,” as they’re called in the Blade Runner universe, which includes the upcoming series Blade Runner 2099, out November 25 on Amazon Prime Video), the 64-year-old global megastar literally wrestles with people and replicants alike on-screen.

Sources indicate that but in real life, she dances with even larger issues. Like what separates humans from the bot world, how we define strength beyond the physical, why we all need to stretch every morning, and, finally, how she gets over a very specific fear. (If you’ve ever watched her in movies like Tomorrow Never Dies or even Everything Everywhere All At Once, you’ll understand how shocking this particular fear is for her. The solution is one six-letter word…and you’ll just have to read on to find out what that is.).

I sat down with Michelle—who is classically trained in ballet and does many of her own martial arts stunts—in NYC for a wide-ranging convo that starts with robots and ends with what she calls the “Michelle prayer.”.

Women’s Health: What was it like to play a replicant, and how did you think about preparing and training for that mindset?

In a recent development, michelle Yeoh: We have a brilliant writer, Silka Luisa, who had thought out the story for Blade Runner 2099 [a continuation of the original series] and where it has gone. All these replicants are now in charge of a Los Angeles that is no longer what we know. But it’s very interesting because [the question that arises is] What is humanity? The replicants do give the humans hope. As long as you’re good, as long as you do things the way we want them to be handled, you could go to a better place, because now Los Angeles is not exactly the most habitable place.

It has been revealed that replicants are made to look human. In fact, they are flesh and blood, except they’re stronger, faster. They are able to withstand the fresh worlds. But empathy is what gives you away as a human. Replicants are born without that emotion. They’re born with memories. They’re given memories to keep them sort of happy and at peace with what they are. Are you born with humanity or does it come with experience and as you live your life with compassion and kindness?

In a recent development, WH: You noted that you’re excited for people to see the series and to share ideas and to talk about it. Is that why? The humanity complexity?

Sources indicate that michelle: The worst is they say, “Oh, yeah, it was interesting.…” What is “just” interesting? Hopefully you go home, you think about it, and then you come back and the next day at work or in school, you’re chatting with your friends— “Well, what are you? A replicant or a human? What would you rather be?”.

WH: How did you prepare, physically, for this role?

Industry observers note that michelle: I think the older you get, the more you have to do to keep up your muscle strength, to keep your muscles there. Without that, you start walking differently. I have the advantage of understanding my body a lot more because I’ve been doing this for the last, well, ever since I was born. I was dancing, doing sports, everything. I do core-strengthening exercises and tai chi every day.

The core was the most notable part of the training because we wanted to nail the way Olwen moved. It was with precision. Because if you want to move with motivation, it has to have that strength, that inner strength, rather than just speed. So when you move, it’s almost like you glide. As a replicant, all the moves are sharp, precise, because they’re so strong and powerful. Actually, when you take a human down, it’s too easy. I think all exercises are core-focused. You can’t lift weights or do pilates without working on the core first. Everything has to start from there.

WH: Has your own relationship to risk changed over the years? Are there stunts that you used to do in your 30s that now you’re like “nah,” or do you actually feel more powerful and in control?

Michelle: I think that’s really interesting and a good way of putting it. Feeling powerful doesn’t mean being reckless and silly. I feel more powerful in the sense that I have a better assessment of the risk factors. But naturally, because when I was in my 20s, when I first started out, you’re brave and foolish and you’re also so fit. And I was really, really, really fit at that time because I didn’t have any crazy injuries. And, so, fearless is a good word, but fearless and stupid is not good. That’s a bad combination.

According to recent reports, sometimes the smallest stunts are the worst because you think they’re easy, and then you don’t pay full attention. You’re not focused enough. You’re focused, but you’re like, “Yeah, yeah, yeah. I’ll get it done.” And that’s when something bad will happen.

In the past, when you are beginning, you listen and you do what they tell you to do, and then you have a lot to prove because you don’t want them to think that you’re unable or you’re not capable, so you do it. But now you go, “How about we…” And then you can speak with power because you know your character. And then I’ll go, “But Olwen won’t do it like that.” And who is going to challenge me?

WH: I understand that you became a bit of a mentor to Hunter Schafer. So talk to us a little about the stunt piece.… Did you help her figure out how to have that voice for herself?

According to recent reports, michelle: To be honest, when I look at her, I go, “Oh my god, I see my young self.” When they show her something, she’ll just throw herself into it because she wants to do it. She’s eager to do it. But then I have to keep reminding her, “You don’t have the same kind of training the stunt people have. So when you can’t do it, it doesn’t mean that you’re not good.”.

Recent findings suggest that what I do is try to remind her, like, “Hunter, knee pads, Hunter, elbow pads. What is the stunt that you’re doing? Get them on.” Because sometimes you go, like, No, no, no, it’s okay. It’s not okay. Get it on.

It’s a joy to work with her. It’s just a joy to be with her, which sometimes can be difficult because we’re supposed to be against each other in Blade Runner 2099. I mean, she’s a human pretending to be a replicant, pretending to be a blade runner. But somehow their missions intertwine, so they have no choice but to learn to work together. So we have a lot of fun.

It has been revealed that WH: What are your nonnegotiables? What are the things you, Michelle, must do every single day for your health that you are consistent with?

Sources indicate that michelle: Water, sunblock, and a lot of stretching. That is a must.

Recent findings suggest that I do tai chi, I do my ballet and tai chi. I’ve been doing that for a long time now. I try to do that every day because I’ve unfortunately had injuries in the past—my back, my knees, my shoulder. I don’t know where I don’t have an injury. As I’m in bed, I do a lot of stretching. When I wake up, the first thing I do in my bed is to go through the motions so that the body wakes up with the mind and everything comes into place.

I think that’s what you have to find: your own moves [or routine] so that you don’t give yourself an excuse when you go, “Oh, it’s raining. No time to go to the gym.” So you just do it even in the bed, you’re stretching, you’re doing all those core exercises to wake up the mind, to wake up the abs, the back, and the legs, everything. And that helps when we’re actually on-set because then I can step into it and know I am strong and ready to go.

I love being outside, going on hikes. Then if I can’t do that, I’m on the elliptical, because I think cardio is still very important. But now, with time, I do a lot more weights. I’m picking up dumbbells or water bottles, whatever works. You have to combine the strengthening of muscles with cardio exercise.

WH: I’m curious if there’s something that is better now in your 60s than it was in your 20s—anything?

Michelle: I think the only thing that’s a little bit better might be this up here [motions to head].

It has been revealed that I do a fairly decent job at keeping up the energy, keeping up the spirits, because I also think it’s the inner strength that is very important. Your mind is very important. If you don’t have the inner peace, it’s very hard to keep control of your body because negative vibes are the worst thing for any human being. When you have negative vibes around you, in you, then you’re down. I honestly believe that because you’ve gone through so many experiences, you’re better for it. I wouldn’t give that up.

In a recent development, michelle: I have a fear of heights. I know. See, I’m claustrophobic and have a fear of heights.

Michelle: But the magic word is action. Camera rolling…action. And I am focused. Fearless. It’s really, really bizarre. If I don’t hear the word action, then it’s a no go. If I’m in the mall, you know, sometimes you have those walkways that look over the first floor. I walk right in the middle of those. I’m taking no risk. But once action is noted on set, I’m good.

WH: You mentioned a mantra. What, exactly, is it?

Michelle: When I wake up, even before opening my eyes and stretching, I sort of have my own little mantra to wake myself up. I try to talk to my body, thank my body, apologize for anything I’ve done bad, and then welcome everything that’s good because I’m deserving of it.

I don’t sit there and meditate. I don’t understand that at all. Just as long as you feel it yourself that I have what I need for me…because everybody is different.

And that’s why I start my day with a prayer, a mantra. I guess you could call it my own Michelle prayer. Be thankful and be willing to accept anything good that comes your way. I think we have to look at ourselves and have self-worth because I think the inner strength, the inner peace, that sense of compassion and kindness and contentment, is very key. Because if you’re always wanting, needing, and thinking about something else, someone else, then you’re always in conflict, first of all, with yourself.

According to recent reports, WH: What does the word strength mean to you? When you hear that word, what’s the definition that comes to mind?

Recent findings suggest that michelle: I think when you hear that word, first of all, it’s always very top layer. You walk into the gym, I have strength, I have power. I put on a power suit. That’s powerful. But for me, true strength is right in there [points to heart]. Showing weakness is strength. Doing a lot of things that people don’t understand, but for you, when you make a choice, it’s strength. There are so many ways of looking at it, and I don’t think there’s one definition unless you check the encyclopedia and they tell you what it is.

WH: And then we’ll just ignore that and go with the Michelle Yeoh definition anyway.

Porsche CEO takes a shot at Tesla’s ‘flying’ Roadster stunt show

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (880 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that tesla’s “flying” Roadster just took a hit from Porsche.
  • Both automakers revealed their next halo cars on the same day, October 15.
  • Recent findings suggest that tesla finally unveiled the next-gen Roadster last month, almost nine years after the 2017 prototype.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that tesla’s “flying” Roadster just took a hit from Porsche. Speaking at a conference in Berlin today, CEO Michael Leiters noted Porsche wants “to completely steer clear from any kind of effects and reveals,” according to Bloomberg.

Both automakers revealed their next halo cars on the same day, October 15. Tesla made a Roadster flip in mid-air. Porsche showed the Mission S, and Leiters says the two cars aren’t even chasing the same customers.

Recent findings suggest that tesla finally unveiled the next-gen Roadster last month, almost nine years after the 2017 prototype. The main event was a car using compressed-air thrusters to launch off a ramp, rotate in the air, and come back down on its wheels.

Sources indicate that it was the payoff for months of hype. Musk spent most of the year promising a “flying” Roadster demo, and it slipped more than once. We reported in June that it had been pushed to August to make room for SpaceX thruster work.

According to recent reports, there are three versions. The Performance trim uses suction fans and claims 0-60 mph in under 1.6 seconds, the Thrust trim adds rear cold-gas thrusters for a claimed sub-0.9-second run, and the single-seat Rocket trim gets thrusters all around the car and isn’t approved for public roads. Tesla gave no price and no production date, just Musk’s “2028, actually.”.

According to recent reports, porsche went the other way. Under the skin, the Mission S can take either a hybrid or a straight combustion powertrain. It’s a mid-engine car that sits above the 911 in the lineup, and well above it in price.

Leiters stated customer response has been “overwhelming” and that Porsche would rather show off real technical innovation than put on a show. If it reaches production, Ferrari is the obvious target, and Porsche hasn’t played in that segment since the 918 Spyder. Porsche is counting on a pricier, more exclusive lineup to rebuild its profits.

Not everyone in the supercar world agrees with Leiters. Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna rated Tesla’s Roadster launch “10 out of 10” last month.

Leiters has a point, even if Porsche pitching a gas and hybrid supercar as “technical innovation” in 2026 is a bit rich. But what bothers me more is who Tesla is aiming at.

I’m concerned Tesla is starting to appeal to the lowest common denominator: people who watch a Roadster hop off a ramp and believe an actual flying car is coming. Musk pushed that idea himself. On Joe Rogan’s show, he called the upcoming demo “unforgettable” and said that if Peter Thiel wants a flying car, “we should be able to buy one.”.

Sources indicate that that’s not real. Cold-gas thrusters work like a giant can of compressed air, and the math is brutal. The Rocket trim carries 400 liters of air at 10,000 psi, roughly 200 kg of gas. At the roughly 80 kN its rear thrusters produce, even a very efficient nozzle empties that tank in a few seconds. Then refilling it takes six to seven hours.

It has been revealed that also someone on Bluesky pointed out that the video shows Mach diamonds in the exhaust stream of the thrusters. Which means it's so loud that anyone within 100 feet would suffer immediate and permanent hearing loss. This Roadster isn't useful for anything other than temporarily pumping stock prices.

Recent findings suggest that so the Roadster’s “flying” will always be limited to stunts like this one. No hopping over traffic. No hovering. A couple of seconds of air, then a long wait at a compressor.

That’s great for a viral clip. But this is a car that dropped from a promised 620 miles of range in 2017 to “over 300” today, and Tesla would rather sell people on a flight the physics can’t deliver.

It’s hard for me to get excited for that. As a BEV enthusiast, I’m not more excited about Porsche’s ICE Mission S, but at least I trust Porsche to actually deliver that to customers.

#6060. Latest Update: What Are Perpetual Futures? How Crypto's Most Popular Derivative Works

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1627 w)
📖 Baca

Latest Update: What Are Perpetual Futures? How Crypto's Most Popular Derivative Works

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1627 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Decrypt

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Perpetual futures are the engine room of crypto trading.
  • They aren't only for crypto, either.
  • This guide explains what futures are, what makes perpetual futures different, how funding rates and liquidations work, and what to know before trading them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Perpetual futures are the engine room of crypto trading. Centralized exchanges processed $85.3 trillion in perps trading volume in 2025 alone, according to CoinGecko's State of Crypto Perpetuals Report 2026, and the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) describes perps as the dominant form of crypto derivatives trading.

They aren't only for crypto, either. Exchanges now offer perps on stocks, commodities and currencies, and Decrypt has become the first news publisher to offer perps trading, powered by Solana exchange Phoenix.

This guide explains what futures are, what makes perpetual futures different, how funding rates and liquidations work, and what to know before trading them.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

To understand perpetual futures, it helps to start with ordinary futures.

A futures contract is an agreement to buy or sell an asset at a set price on a set date in the future. Futures have been used for centuries: farmers used them to lock in prices for crops before harvest, and today they are traded on everything from oil and wheat to stock indexes and Bitcoin, on regulated exchanges such as CME.

Industry observers note that traders use futures for two main reasons. Hedgers use them to protect against price swings; an airline might buy oil futures to lock in fuel costs, for example. Speculators use them to bet on price movements without owning the underlying asset.

Traditional futures have an expiry date. When a contract expires, it settles, either by delivering the asset or, more often, by paying out the difference in cash. Traders who want to keep their position open must "roll" it into a latest contract, which can add costs and complexity.

In a recent development, perpetual futures, often shortened to "perps" or "perpetual swaps," work like futures, but with one key difference: they never expire. Traders can hold a position for as long as they like, provided they have enough collateral to keep it open.

According to recent reports, the idea was proposed by Yale economist Robert Shiller in a 1993 paper as a way to create markets for assets that are hard to trade directly. Perps took off in crypto. Crypto exchange BitMEX, widely credited with bringing perps to crypto, launched a perpetual contract on Bitcoin in 2016. BitMEX itself closed in September 2026, but the product it pioneered has become the most traded instrument in crypto.

A perpetual contract never actually involves owning the asset. Traders deposit collateral, or "margin," and their profit or loss depends entirely on how the price moves.

According to recent reports, when opening a perp position, a trader chooses a direction. Going long means betting the price will rise; going short means betting it will fall. Being able to short as easily as going long is one reason perps are popular: it lets traders profit from falling prices, or hedge assets they already own.

Perps are usually traded with leverage, which lets traders control a larger position than their collateral alone would allow. With 10x leverage, for example, $100 of margin controls a $1,000 position. If the asset's price rises 5%, the trader makes $50, a 50% return on their margin. But if it falls 5%, they lose $50, half of their margin.

In a recent development, exchanges track two prices to manage this. The index price is the asset's price on spot markets, usually averaged across several exchanges. The mark price, based on the index and the perp market itself, is used to calculate profits and losses and to decide when positions must be closed. Using an averaged price makes it harder for a sudden spike on one exchange to trigger liquidations.

Because perps never expire, nothing forces their price to converge with the underlying asset, as traditional futures do at expiry. Instead, perps use a funding rate.

At regular intervals—most commonly every eight hours, though some platforms use shorter or longer schedules—traders on one side of the market pay traders on the other:.

Decentralized exchange Hyperliquid, for example, pays funding every hour, at one-eighth of the rate calculated for an eight-hour period, to stay consistent with centralized exchanges.

In a recent development, funding payments go directly between traders, not to the exchange. For traders holding positions over long periods, these payments can add up, and they can either boost or erode returns.

Funding rates also offer a window into market sentiment. Strongly positive funding suggests traders are crowded into bullish bets, while negative funding shows that bears are paying to stay short.

Rates for the same asset can also differ between exchanges. On November 19, 2026, Bitcoin's funding rate was 0.01% per eight hours on Hyperliquid, compared with 0.0037% on Binance, according to Hyperliquid's funding comparison tool.

According to recent reports, some traders aim to earn funding payments rather than bet on prices. In a "cash and carry" or basis trade, they buy an asset on the spot market and short the same amount through perps, collecting funding while their positions offset each other's price moves.

According to recent reports, leverage is a double-edged sword. Every perp position has a maintenance margin, the minimum collateral needed to keep it open. If losses push a trader's margin below that level, the exchange automatically closes the position, a process called liquidation. The trader typically loses most or all of the margin they put up.

Sources indicate that the higher the leverage, the smaller the price move needed to trigger a liquidation. At 50x leverage, a 2% move against a position can wipe it out.

Sources indicate that liquidations can also feed on each other. When prices fall sharply, liquidated longs are forced to sell, pushing prices lower and triggering further liquidations, a so-called liquidation cascade. On October 10, 2025, the crypto market saw its largest liquidation event on record, with more than $19 billion in leveraged positions wiped out in a single day.

To cover losses when positions can't be closed in time, exchanges typically keep an insurance fund. In extreme cases, some use auto-deleveraging, closing profitable positions on the other side of the market to keep the system solvent.

Crypto perps trade on two main types of venue.

Recent findings suggest that centralized exchanges, such as Binance, Bybit and OKX, run their own order books and hold users' funds. They account for the vast majority of perps trading: Binance alone held about a third of centralized perps volume in early 2026, according to CoinGecko. Many are unavailable to U.S. customers.

According to recent reports, decentralized exchanges let traders use perps through smart contracts, while keeping control of their funds. Some, such as Hyperliquid and Solana-based Phoenix, run order books onchain, matching buyers and sellers much like a traditional exchange. Others, such as GMX and Jupiter, let traders trade against a shared pool of liquidity provided by other users.

Sources indicate that decentralized perps are growing fast. Their trading volume jumped from $1.5 trillion in 2024 to $6.38 trillion in 2025, led by Hyperliquid, CoinGecko found. Decentralized exchanges' share of perps trading volume peaked at 13% in late 2025 before slipping to 10% in April 2026, while their share of open interest, the total value of open positions, reached 13.5%.

Industry observers note that in the U.S., perps developed largely on offshore exchanges, outside the reach of the CFTC, but that has started to change. In July 2025, Coinbase introduced CFTC-regulated "perpetual-style" futures for U.S. customers, with five-year expiries and up to 10x leverage. Two months later, CFTC-regulated exchange Bitnomial launched what it called the first U.S. perpetual futures, with 25-year terms and eight-hour funding. In May 2026, the CFTC approved a Bitcoin perpetual futures contract from prediction market Kalshi and set out a framework for listing more, and in June, Kraken rolled out perps to eligible U.S. customers through Bitnomial, which its parent manufacturer had acquired.

Some of these contracts, including Kalshi's and Bitnomial's original design, have long but fixed terms of 25 years, so are not strictly perpetual. The regulator states perps can be offered on CFTC-registered exchanges under federal oversight, and has advised U.S. traders to avoid offshore venues.

It has been revealed that the shift has been contested. CME Group, the largest U.S. futures exchange, has sued the CFTC, arguing that perps are swaps rather than futures under U.S. law. The CFTC has nonetheless continued to approve more perps platforms, starting with Backpack.

Perps are now spreading beyond crypto. Exchanges have begun listing perps tracking stocks, stock indexes, commodities such as gold and oil, and currencies, giving traders around-the-clock exposure to markets that normally close in the evening and on weekends.

Industry observers note that those products carry the same mechanics, and the same risks, as crypto perps. They track an asset's price without giving traders ownership of the asset itself, so a perp on a manufacturer's stock doesn't come with voting rights or dividends.

Perps can be useful tools for hedging and speculation, but they are among the riskiest products in crypto:.

It has been revealed that decrypt customers can now trade perps directly alongside the news, through the Decrypt Money Account. The service is powered by Phoenix, a decentralized exchange on Solana, and lets users go long or short on crypto, stocks and commodities.

Availability varies by region, and as with any leveraged product, traders should only risk money they can afford to lose.
